news.title: Conservative Gubernatorial Candidate Rebecca Bextel Warns Wyoming Could Become Like Colorado If It Departs From ‘Bread And Butter’ Policies
news.text:
Third-party Wyoming gubernatorial candidate Rebecca Bextel told Tucker Carlson during an interview released Saturday that the Republican Party has “imploded” in the state.

Bextel, a former Republican committeewoman who is running under the Constitution Party to be the next governor of the Equality State, cited the late Charlie Kirk’s June 2020 warning during the interview that the state will become “blue” because Democrats will have infiltrated the Republican Party. She notably accused Republican gubernatorial nominee Eric Barlow of being an example of that. (RELATED: How The Left Is Taking Over America’s Reddest State)

Neither Bextel nor Barlow immediately responded to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s requests for comment.

“And so what happens is the Democrats, they really have no say in Wyoming politics, so they all switch over to the Republican Party. We always have conservatives that split the election for the primary and then we end up with the Democrat candidate,” Bextel said. “And that’s exactly what’s happening right now.”

Barlow beat President Donald Trump’s endorsed candidate, Megan Degenfelder, for the Republican gubernatorial nomination on Aug. 18.

“Our candidate for the Republican Party won’t even sign platform pledge to say that they’ll stick with the party 80% of the time,” Bextel continued. “This guy is so radical. He actually testified in front of Congress one time and said we needed to remove our dependence on fossil fuels in favor of a renewable energy model. So, can you imagine a guy like that being in charge of Wyoming, where our bread and butter is the mineral industry and the energy sector?”

Wyoming is the largest coal-producing state in the nation and also has more oil and natural gas producing leases on federal lands than any other state, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. As such, its four leading sources of revenue in 2026 included $12.4 billion from oil drilling and gas extraction, $4.1 billion from petroleum refining, $3.8 billion from gasoline and petroleum bulk stations, and $3.4 billion from coal mining, according to IBISWorld.

“Well … he’s funded by the Democrats — the dark, George Soros-funded money,” Bextel said when Carlson asked how a candidate like that gets the Republican nomination. “That has trickled its way into Wyoming. We’re a very cheap state to buy politically. So, you know, if you look at someone like Vivek Ramaswamy running a 100-million-dollar governor run, I’ll be lucky if I raise a million bucks. But that’s what I’m taking on.”

“He’s not a Republican,” she also said. “And so, I’m running to basically save us from turning into the state of Colorado. If I lose this election, we will be Colorado in four years.”

Trump won Wyoming 72.3% to 26.1% against former Vice President Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential election.

“They just vote for the Republican because that’s who you vote for … they don’t know,” Carlson observed.

Bextel responded by telling him that that’s why she’s been “begging people, ‘Please don’t vote for the R.’”

“The Republican Party has imploded,” Bextel continued. “It’s not just imploded nationally, it’s imploded in Wyoming. We don’t have any leadership. People would prefer the values of the Republican Party, but there’s no litmus test, Tucker, to just put an ‘R’ by your name.”

“Yes,” Tucker responded.

Bextel resigned from being the Teton County Republican Party’s state committeewoman in May 2026. She previously ran for chair of the Wyoming Republican Party in 2025.

“We have tons of people, like in Teton County: a guy will run as a Democrat for county commissioner, lose. Run again as a Democrat, lose,” Bextel said. “Then go do something different, put an ‘R’ by his name, lose, and then join the board of the Teton County Republican Party. It doesn’t make any sense … We have to put the person above the party, and that’s what I’m asking everyone to do in Wyoming.”
news.summary: ‘We have to put the person above the party’
news.author: Spencer Lombardo

news.title: ‘No line he will not cross’: Obama slams Ramaswamy’s ‘cruel’ ad, hits out at Trump
news.text: Former US President Barack Obama has criticised President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, accusing them of abandoning basic standards of decency as he campaigned for Democratic candidates in Ohio ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.Obama focused much of his criticism on Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has continued to defend an advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Dr Amy Acton. Trump and vice president JD Vance have also defended the campaign, despite calls from prominent Ohio Republicans, including governor Mike DeWine, to withdraw it."In recent days, we have seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy. He noted that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she has experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness"."There is a decency we should expect out of our public officials," Obama continued. "And I do not know what has happened where the standards of behaviour are so low that somebody could run an ad like that."Acton accuses Ramaswamy of exploiting her childhoodActon, who appeared alongside Obama, directly challenged Ramaswamy over the advertisement, accusing him of using her personal history to rescue his campaign."My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it is not going to work," she said. "Decency still matters."She added: "Mr Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you will not stoop."Ramaswamy has defended the advertisement as legitimate campaign material, while the controversy has intensified an already closely fought election in Ohio.Obama also criticised Trump over the cost of living, saying the president had failed to deliver on a key campaign promise to make life more affordable. Instead, he pointed to Trump's focus on renovating the White House, including plans for a new ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn."I do not know if you have noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," Obama quipped. "He should be on HGTV."He went on, "There is gold everywhere. He is got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."Obama campaigns across key battleground statesObama, 65, remains a prominent campaigner for the Democratic Party and was due to travel to Michigan later on Saturday to support Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official running against Republican former Representative Mike Rogers.El-Sayed won a divisive Democratic primary by less than one percentage point. Obama's appearance in Detroit, a city with a predominantly Black population, could help El-Sayed strengthen his support among Black voters. During the primary, his rival Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about six percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for El-Sayed in September.El-Sayed has previously criticised Obama's record, arguing in 2012 that the former president had failed to fulfil all his progressive campaign promises. He wrote that Obama "was not the right choice -- he just wasn't the wrong one".However, El-Sayed later described Obama as "foundational" to his decision to enter politics, while acknowledging that he still disagreed with parts of the former president's record.Michigan also has competitive elections for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson is facing Republican Representative John James.In Ohio, Obama appeared with Acton and former Senator Sherrod Brown, who is seeking to unseat Republican Senator Jon Husted. Trump and Vance have visited the state in recent weeks to campaign for Husted and Ramaswamy.Obama is also scheduled to headline a rally in Georgia next week with Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is due to speak in Georgia on Saturday.Obama urges voters to reject Republican leadershipAcknowledging that Trump would remain president for another two years, until his term ends, Obama urged voters to use the midterm elections to challenge Republican leaders."We are not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said."After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence ... you get a chance to say enough is enough."You use AI every day. news.title: Obama set to spend Saturday on the Democratic campaign trail ahead of midterms
news.text:
Barack Obama will campaign Saturday alongside Democratic candidates for the U.S. Senate in Ohio and Michigan, two competitive states that will help determine control of the chamber, as the former president steps up his role in the midterm elections.

Obama’s first appearance is in Cleveland with former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is attempting to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted. 

Amy Acton, a Democrat campaigning for governor against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, is also set to join the event.

Although Ohio has shifted more reliably Republican, it has been a fiercely contested battleground this year.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to rally support for Husted and Ramaswamy.

Obama will then travel to Detroit for a rally with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official working to unify Michigan’s Democratic base after winning a competitive primary by under a percentage point. 

El-Sayed is running against Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers.

Obama’s visit to Detroit, which is three-quarters Black, could help build support for El-Sayed among Black voters. 

During the primary, opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. 

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.

El-Sayed offered criticism of Obama after his 2012 reelection over unfulfilled progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama "was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one."

El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month he valued the former president, calling him "foundational" to his path to run for office, though noting elements of Obama's presidency he differed with.

"It’s a normal thing to love somebody, to really appreciate all that they’ve done, and to say, ‘Hey, here are some things I would have done differently,’" El-Sayed said. "But they still did some important things to create opportunity for you."

El-Sayed spoke with Obama on the phone shortly after winning his primary in August.

Michigan also has open contests for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Democratic nominee for governor Jocelyn Benson is slated to appear with others down the ballot. Benson faces Republican Rep. John James.

Obama will lead a rally in Georgia next week alongside Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is scheduled to speak in Georgia on Saturday.

news.title: There Was Only One Way the Democrats Could Blow the Midterms — and Lord Help ‘Em, They’re Doing It!
news.text:
Forget about packing the Supreme Court, banning ICE, or impeaching the president (again): Should they win congress, the Democrats’ shrewdest move would be moving Election Day to September.

‘Cause if elections were held in September, the Democrats would be undefeated. They’d go from the donkeys to the ’72 Dolphins. The Democrats would run the whole country!

But alas, they always peak too early.

Fun fact: In the last FIVE presidential elections, during the month of September, the Democrats have led the “poll of polls” aggregate every flippin’ time.

It’s become a clear PR pattern: The Democrats build momentum, blitz the media, and peak in popularity before Election Day — and sometimes, they’re so far ahead that the Republicans can’t catch up. Sure, the race tightens down the stretch (uncomfortably so), but the Dems still win.

But an awful lot of the time, the donkeys are gassed. There’s nothing left in the tank. 

So their momentum stalls — and the Republicans soar ahead by the first Tuesday of November. The Dems are all out of ammo, all out of energy, and all out of ideas. Victory slips through their fingers hooves.

And once again, the Republicans control the White House, Senate, and/or the House.

That's psychologically unnerving for the Democrats, because they really, truly believe their own press clippings: Everyone hates Trump. Everyone thinks they ought to be in charge. Everything they see, hear, and read reinforces how wonderful they are.

This election belongs to the Democrats!

Then, when they lose, resentment builds. They blame the voters, blame the consultants, blame the DNC, blame Elon Musk’s space lasers, blame Russia, blame social media — and blame everyone but themselves.

Yet this pattern persists, because the Dems won’t address the root cause. (Which is the best possible news for the GOP.)

Because don’t look now, but the donkeys are doing it again: They’re making the exact same mistake — and this time, it could cost them the 2026 midterms.

Between the historic headwinds, President Donald Trump’s dismal approval rating, and sky-high gas prices, the Democrats should win the midterms by a landslide. Since 1934, the president’s party has lost an average of 27 House seats and 3.4 Senate seats in midterm elections. By each and every current metric and historic benchmark, the Democrats should be dominating. 

So the 2026 midterms ought to be a big, beautiful, Blue Tsunami: They’re the ocean; congress is Atlantis.

That’s the Democrats’ expectation — and the catalyst for their error.

The danger in believing your own press clippings is that it distorts your perspective. You overestimate your own popularity, capabilities, and value, which leads to hubris and overreach.

And you also underestimate your opponent.

In Hollywood, it’s why so many celebs crash and burn. On Wall Street, it’s why so many corporations botch acquisitions, misjudge verticals, and lose money on mergers.

And in politics, it’s why the Democrats can’t resist scaring the [expletive] out of the voters.

Because it’s late October, and the Democrats are struggling yet again. They’re gassed. Even in bright blue states such as Michigan, Minnesota, Maine, and New Hampshire, the Republican Senate candidate is either winning outright or within the margin of error. 

There’s a very real risk the Dems could lose all four elections!

The Democrats had a glide path to victory: Don’t be controversial. Don’t interject divisive issues. No trans or wokeisms. Make the election a litmus test on Donald Trump.

The last one was the motherlode. The Democrats already had all the leftists, party loyalists, DSA acolytes, and Trump-haters in their pocket, but if they could position themselves as a vehicle to “send D.C. a message,” they’d gain all the dissatisfied independents, too.

Including those who disagreed with the Democrats’ policies.

Hey, it’s how MAGA ran the table in 2024: Not everyone who voted for Trump supported his platform, either. Plenty voted Republican because Joe Biden’s senility, DNC corruption, and Kamala Harris’ weirdness repulsed them.

The voters wanted a change; Trump was it. He was the “send D.C. a message” candidate. 

The Democrats keep fading down the stretch because they really, truly believe their own press clippings. After all, their friends in the media keep telling them the same thing: Trump is awful, everyone hates him, the future belongs to the donkeys.

Then they see the September polls: Why, they’re cruising to victory, winning in a cakewalk. 

It’s not even close!

(No wonder they trust the polls: Not only do they say really nice things about the Dems, but they actually PAID for a lot of ‘em!)

So the candidates see the polls and are emboldened. That’s problematic, but a disciplined candidate should still be able to stick to a script. (Mostly.) 

The bigger problem is that the activists are emboldened, too. They count their chickens before they’re hatched, demanding a wish-list of left-wing policies, revenge fantasies, and political grievances — i.e. packing the Supreme Court, impeaching the president, jailing Republicans, disbanding ICE, banning billionaires, and killing the AI industry.

Historically, left-wing activists have damaged the Democratic brand more than ANYTHING Donald Trump has EVER done. They’re the GOP’s best friends.

Fast forward to 2026: Once again, the Dems dominated the month of September. (As well as August: Over the past eight years, about 70% of August polls have overestimated support for Democrats.) Once again, the Democrats have swallowed the hype.

And once again, the activists have gotten greedy.

Because of the media’s focus, left-wing rhetoric, and activist overreach, the public face of the 2026 midterms isn’t Donald Trump anymore. It certainly was in August and September, but we’re now in late October.

The public face of the 2026 midterms is now Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Ilhan Omar Ilhan Nur Said Elmi (D-Minn.)

El-Sayed simply can’t resist detonating rhetorical landmines. He has the self-restraint of a Charlie Sheen on a bender — and is terrifying normie Americans. The more media attention he absorbs, the worse it is for the rest of the Democratic Party.

Trouble is, he’s about to absorb even more: He’s attending a campaign rally Saturday with Barack Obama.

And Omar’s “not to my knowledge” gaffe when quizzed about the possibility she married her brother (!) was a gift from the political gods.

news.title: There’s a Huge Reason Why You Shouldn't Believe the Midterm Polls
news.text:
Democrats are acting as if Senate control is within their grasp, but John McLaughlin, a longtime pollster for President Donald Trump, says the surveys feeding that confidence are badly skewed.

With less than two weeks until Election Day, McLaughlin warned that the 2026 midterms are extremely close, and that some polls appear to deliberately shortchange Republicans by shrinking their share of the sample. Appearing Friday on Just the News, No Noise, he pointed to a New York poll in which just 22% of respondents were Republican. In the state's last gubernatorial race, Republicans made up 30% of the people who actually voted.

That's an eight-point hole for the GOP before a single question gets asked.

Asked how that happens, McLaughlin pointed the finger at the press.

"I think it's deliberate because a lot of the media that covers those polls has a bias," McLaughlin said.

He also had a word for the gatekeepers who decide which polls get treated as gospel and which get dismissed.

"Sometimes they don't put the liberal pollsters through the same kind of scrutiny," he added.

The consequences reach well beyond cable news narratives, too. "It affects donors," McLaughlin explained. A Republican donor who keeps hearing that a race is slipping away has every reason to hold onto his checkbook, and a self-fulfilling prophecy is a lot cheaper for Democrats than an actual campaign.

ICYMI: Still Think Talarico Will Flip Texas? You Might Want to Read This.

We've seen Republican support underestimated before, and McLaughlin walked through the track record. "Remember when there was a Hillary lock in 2016," he said. "Remember when there was going to be a [Joe] Biden blue wave in 2020, and remember [former] Vice President Kamala Harris at this point in time in 2024."

He sees the same pattern repeating now.

"So there's been, you know, a lot of bad calls, bad polling, and it seems like they're doubling down on the bad polls in this election cycle because when you get into the internals of the polls, they just don't make sense," McLaughlin continued. "They don't match up with the electorate, what they're going to look like in a midterm election."

Texas offers a perfect example.

In 2024, multiple polls showed Trump with a mere four-point lead over Kamala Harris in Texas. Trump ultimately won the state by 14 points. McLaughlin suggested the same thing could be happening in the Texas Senate race, where some polls show Texas State Rep. James Talarico (D-50th District) beating Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.

I, for one, am not buying the Texas flip narrative.

Talarico's polling lead deserves attention, but Texas is a Republican state, and even MS NOW’s Katy Tur is skeptical of the polls saying Talarico is ahead.

Even CNN's Harry Enten has admitted that polling averages in close Senate races have historically missed the final result by an average of 3.7 points, and since 2016, those misses have mostly favored Republicans. A GOP over-performance of that size would deliver a 52-48 Republican majority.

So who exactly are the polls missing? Pollster Frank Luntz says Republican voters are simply less willing to sit through surveys. If those voters keep hanging up on pollsters and then show up on Election Day anyway, the results could look very different from what the media is promising.

But let’s be clear: McLaughlin isn't predicting a cakewalk for either side.

"I've never seen it so close," he said. "There are eight Senate races that are toss-ups. [In] the House, there's over 70 seats in play. There's 17, at least pure toss-ups. So it really is a toss-up election."

In the end, all we know is that polls are snapshots built on assumptions, and those assumptions often turn out to be wrong. Republicans who tune out the doom and simply show up have the power to make them wrong again.

news.title: Fox's complicated relationship with Donald Trump: The Katie Zacharia death trap exposed how close the President keeps his friends at the network... but he has a hit list of ememies, too
news.text:
Donald Trump had a problem – and he knew just the person to solve it.

His new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, was floundering after a mere four days on the job. It was devastatingly clear that the hasty hire had been a mistake. So somehow – exactly how remains unclear – word reached Sean Hannity's ear that he was free on his Fox show to deliver the death blow.

Why did you claim repeatedly that you were an attorney, Hannity asked a visibly stunned Zacharia, who had evidently expected a softball redemptive chat. Why did you take so few questions?

'Somebody at the White House set her up for a trap in that interview,' a senior administration official told the Daily Mail last week, adding that it was likely either Trump himself or his chief of staff, Susie Wiles.

'It only could have been Susie or the president himself. Nobody else is going to be able to make that call to Hannity.'

After the shambolic Hannity interview on Thursday night, and an equally dismal follow-up Friday morning, Trump had the excuse he needed to fire Zacharia.

'You don't have to do this if you don't want to,' Trump told Zacharia. 'Honestly if I were you, I'd reconsider.'

Trump signed the death warrant; Fox News was the messenger. So, was he happy with the network? Well, not publicly. 

On Monday morning, the president was raging against them. 

'Fox spends more time defending Dumocrats, and putting on their views versus their Republican opponent, than at any time in the History of FoxNews,' he wrote on Truth Social. 'It's ridiculous! FoxNews is trying too hard to be Politically Correct!'

Truth be told, Trump's relationship with the network has always been complicated.

On October 4, he was mourning the departure of his ally Maria Bartiromo, a 12-year veteran of the network who, according to the Murdoch-owned Wall Street Journal, left the company when executives became alarmed by her allegedly sharing broadcast plans with the White House. Bartiromo's attorney denied that she was fired and claimed in a statement at the time of her departure that she was 'still employed by Fox.'

Trump said he missed her, railing in a lengthy post about the executives who chose not to cover his midterm rallies.

'Who makes these decisions at Fox News?' he wrote on Truth Social. 'Probably the same loser that fired the great Maria Bartiromo because she complained about not being allowed to cover "TRUMP." She'll end up bigger and better than ever - watch!'

So, who can Trump rely on at the network and whose fealty is rather less constant? Here, the Daily Mail provides a run-down of the stars.

AINSLEY EARHARDT

The 50-year-old Fox and Friends co-host, engaged to Sean Hannity, is as loyal to the president as her fiancé, and can be relied on to tamp down any criticism from guests or fellow hosts.

The closest she has come to taking Trump to task was perhaps in June this year, when she asked foreign correspondent Trey Yingst: 'Trey, what do you say to our viewers who love Donald Trump and support him and trust him… but they're tired of this, and they see that the midterms are around the corner, they want our economy to get back on track and our gas prices to drop. What do we need to do to get out?'

The president has also made no secret of his admiration for Earhardt, frequently promoting her children's books and gently teasing her about her relationship with Hannity.

When the pair announced their engagement, in December 2024, he wrote on social media: 'Great news about Sean and Ainsley. They are officially engaged to be married! There are no finer people than these, and there will be no finer couple. A deal made in HEAVEN!!!'

SEAN HANNITY

Chief among the high-profile coterie of die-hard Trump loyalists is Sean Hannity, the highest paid news anchor on television, who takes home an estimated $25 million a year.

Hannity, 64, the longest running cable news host in television history, is open about being a friend of the president's: Earlier this month he told USA Today that he and Trump's relationship 'goes back way before he ever thought about politics.'

But he added, his approach as an interviewer is to simply 'let him talk.'

The pair, both New Yorkers, have known each other for 30 years.

During his first term, Trump was so frequently on the phone to Hannity that his aides referred to the television star as 'the unofficial chief of staff,' according to the Washington Post.

One advisor told the paper in 2018: 'He basically has a desk in the place.'

That close connection is evidently as strong as ever.

JESSE WATTERS

Jesse Watters, 48, is another fierce defender of Trump's, brushing off the president's controversial comments as jokes and defending him as a man with a sense of humor.

When Trump, earlier this month, commented approvingly on the physique of Ohio's incumbent senator, Jon Hustead, Watters leapt to his defense.

'We're talking about guys' a***s,' said Watters. 'Trump says a lot of stuff we all think and we don't say. Sometimes it sounds a little gay. He can get away with it because he's straight.'

When Trump said he would be 'a dictator on day one,' Watters dismissed it as a joke.

And when Trump lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden, Watters soothingly said that Trump was 'a legend no matter what happens.'

The admiration appears mutual.

When Trump raged this week against the Washington DC judge who concluded that the Reflecting Pool was left murky by shoddy installation rather than vandalism, Trump said the judge should have watched Watters.

The president wrote on Truth Social that 'some Radical Left person in the DC US Attorney's Office' had 'got it wrong and obviously didn't investigate, witness or see the attached tape, or the very inspiring Jesse Watters show which explained it all.'

Yet there is a growing sense, perhaps, that Hannity, Watters and their allies are increasingly outnumbered by those actually willing to challenge Trump.

ON THE FENCE

Bret Baier, the widely respected chief political anchor, won plaudits for his June 2023 interview with Trump in which he pressed the then former president about his handling of classified documents.

'I want to go through the boxes and get all my personal things out,' said Trump, effectively admitting he had documents he knew did not belong to him. 'I don't want to hand that over to [the National Archives] yet.'

Baier, in a July 2025 discussion with The New Yorker editor David Remnick, laughingly noted that Trump 'called it a nasty interview afterwards.'

'I've always, every time I've interviewed him, taken it as a tough but fair effort,' said Baier. 'He has called me - "You know what Bret, you're a five, four, nowhere near a seven."'

Baier, 56, sprang to national prominence following the 9/11 attacks.

At the time he was working as a correspondent in Fox's Atlanta bureau and was dispatched to the Pentagon. Fox executives were impressed and made him the Pentagon correspondent.

In 2009, he took over the nightly show Special Report from his mentor Brit Hume and has been hosting the hour-long program ever since.

Baier's close relationship with Trump has seen him come in for criticism, but he insists his rounds of golf with the president give him enviable insight.

'Tell me the journalist that won't take the three-hour off-the-record ability to pick the brain of the commander-in-chief, the president, who's making these big decisions, in an environment that is more relaxed - that perhaps he's more open to talking about different things, to get you a sense of where his head is in the middle of all these big things,' said Baier.

'Tell me that journalist who doesn't take that, and I'll say, I don't know who turns it down.'

Earlier this month, Baier told Vanity Fair that he did not give Trump 'a pass' when it came to contentious issues but rather gave him time to explain his opinion.

'We definitely have to cover it and have on the critics of how he operates, but also listen to the administration's side, because what Donald Trump says is one thing, and things that he does are another thing,' said Baier.

Asked what he makes of Trump's battle over the Kennedy Center, Baier told the magazine: 'It's a fascinating story.'

LAURA INGRAHAM 

A former speechwriter for the Reagan administration, Laura Ingraham clerked for Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas in the early 1990s before entering conservative media.

In 1999, 'just starting out in the media,' Ingraham met Donald Trump for lunch in New York, she told the Katie Miller podcast.

Ingraham, 63, said she had this idea of Trump as a celebrity with a giant ego, and was 'just kind of rolling my eyes' before their meeting at Le Cirque.

'But I was so shocked that during this lunch he talked nothing about himself,' said Ingraham. 'All he wanted to do was find out: how do you make your money in radio? How do you get commercials? He was mapping my whole business out.'

At the end of the lunch, he lent her his car for the afternoon to explore New York – adding: 'Make sure you take these hand wipes with you, because New York is filthy.'

She told Miller: 'We still joke about that.'

The two have remained firm friends, with Ingraham being widely discussed as a possible press secretary for his first term.

In December 2016, she said on air: 'I have known Donald Trump for a long time, and we have been friends for a long time, and I am looking forward to that conversation. It is a great privilege to even be considered.

'If your country calls you, if God opens that door, you have to seriously consider it. If I can really help, it is hard to say no to that. If I think I can help, which I think I could.'

The job ultimately went to Sean Spicer.

Ingraham, however, remained an influential advisor, regularly consulted by the president – and close to his children.

In October last year it was announced that Ingraham had gone into business with Donald Trump Jr, sitting on the board of investment firm Colombier Acquisition Corp III.

The Connecticut-born host has, however, been critical of the Iran war, asking Trump in an interview at the Republican National Convention how Iran was still able to get missiles.

'I thought we decimated them?' she asked him, adding: 'If we hadn't done Iran, you'd be cruising to midterm victory.'

HARRIS FAULKNER

Atlanta-born Harris Faulkner, 61, joined Fox News in 2005 and is known as a reliable proponent of the president's views.

The closest she came to criticism was in 2020, when Trump was angered by the George Floyd protests and unrest, and tweeted: 'When the looting starts, the shooting starts'.

Harris, in an interview with Trump in June 2020, told him: 'I'm Harris on TV, but I'm a black woman. I'm a mom. And you've talked about it, but we haven't seen you come out and be that consoler in this instance. And the tweets, "when the looting starts, the shooting starts." Why those words?'

He said he had heard it from 'a very tough mayor.'

Faulkner then corrected him.

'No. It comes from 1967. I was about 18 months old at the time. But it was from the chief of police in Miami. He was cracking down, and he meant what he said. And he said, "I don't even care if it makes it look like brutality I'm going to crack down, when the looting starts, the shooting starts."'

'That frightened a lot of people when you tweeted that.'

BRIAN KILMEADE

One Fox stalwart who has become noticeably more critical of Trump is Brian Kilmeade, who was extremely supportive of the Iran war this spring, and yet is now taking the president to task for his Russia policy.

Kilmeade, 62, who has been at Fox News since its October 1996 birth, strongly condemned last week Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel, accusing the president of appeasing 'the modern Hitler.'

Kilmeade, fired up, told his rather surprised-looking co-hosts on October 11 that Trump was enabling Vladimir Putin, describing the Russian leader as 'the cause of all the problems in the region,' who 'now is helping Iran, will kill our guys and blow up our bases.'

Kilmeade's hawkish views on Russia and support for Ukraine are not, in themselves, new.

But his strident condemnation of the president's actions, with less than a month to go until the midterms, certainly raised eyebrows.

Further unwelcome criticism came the following day, when Mark Levin, usually a Trump stalwart, on Monday disavowed Trump's call for Volodymyr Zelensky to hold elections.

'When will Putin have real elections?' wrote Levin on X, retweeting a post from a Hudson Institute academic arguing against demanding elections in Ukraine.

'He's been running Russia a lot longer than Zelensky has been president of Ukraine,' Levin continued. 'The same can be said about the Arab countries and more.'

JACQUI HEINRICH

Even more strident are reporters Jennifer Griffin who covers the Pentagon, and Jacqui Heinrich who reports from the White House.

Both women are undaunted about taking Trump to task, with Heinrich, 37, infuriating Trump by immediately rebutting his November 2020 claim that the voting machines were rigged against him.

She has continued with her no-holds-barred reporting in the president's second term, pointedly remarking that the Alaska summit between Trump and Putin of August 2025 did not go well for the US leader.

'The way that it felt in the room was not good,' she said while live on air. 'It did not seem like things went well, and it seemed like Putin came in and steamrolled, got right into what he wanted to say, and got his photo next to the president and then left.'

Her comments quickly went viral, with John Oliver mockingly noting that Trump 'held a press conference that went so badly even this Fox News reporter couldn't put a positive spin on it.'

JENNIFER GRIFFIN

Griffin, 57, has been equally searing, taking Trump to task in recent months over the Iran war.

When a Tomahawk missile hit a girls' school in Iran on the first day of air strikes, and Trump tried to say perhaps another country used the weapons (the UK, Australia, Netherlands and Japan are the only nations beside the US with Tomahawks), Griffin said that Trump was attempting to 'muddy the waters.'

When the administration attempted to subpoena reporters over their stories about the Qatari gift plane and the drama surrounding Air Force One, Griffin said the threats to the journalists 'should alarm every American.'

Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war, called her a 'Trump hater.'

MARTHA MACCALLUM

New Jersey-born Martha MacCallum, 62, worked as a financial reporter for Wall Street Journal Television and CNBC before joining Fox in 2004.

Seen as a safe pair of hands, she has throughout both Trump's terms carved out a niche hosting town halls and debates.

Her questioning has at times angered the president.

In September 2024, asked on Fox and Friends whether he would want to accept Fox's offer to host a second debate with Kamala Harris, he replied: 'Well, I wouldn't want to have Martha and Bret. I'd love to have somebody else other than Martha and Bret. I'd love to have, frankly, Sean or Jesse or Laura. You know, somebody else. Let's give other people a shot.'

He added: 'But I didn't think Martha and Bret were so good last night. Jesse was fantastic last night. What he said, Jesse. Really got it. Jesse said to Trump once: that debate that was, we won that debate by a lot. And I wouldn't want Martha involved.'

And earlier this month, he was infuriated by MacCallum interviewing Michigan senate contender Abdul el-Sayed, a Democrat.

'FoxNews spends more time covering the Jihadist and Dumocrat candidates than they do the good old fashioned Republicans, the people that have saved America, and are making it great again,' he complained on October 6. 'All they talk about is Dumocrat Jihadists like El-Sayed, with his softball interview by Martha MacCallum, and the like. She never interviews me like that.'

Fox did not respond to the Daily Mail's request for comment.
news.summary: Who can Trump rely on at Fox News and whose fealty is rather less constant? The Daily Mail provides a run-down of the network's stars and their stance.

news.text: Former US vice president Kamala Harris has returned to the campaign trail to support Democrats in closely contested races ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, as speculation grows over whether she will make another bid for the White House in 2028.According to news agency Reuters, Harris, the Democratic Party's 2024 presidential nominee, is campaigning in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. She has made relatively few public appearances this year but is now stepping up efforts to help Democrats challenge Republican control of Congress.Harris began her campaign tour in Las Vegas on Tuesday, criticising President Donald Trump and his administration over what she described as its cruelty and incompetence. Campaigning for lefty candidates all over the country sure does work up an appetite. 

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez jumped off the trail to visit an In-N-Out burger after holding an event in Bakersfield, Calif., as part of a nationwide tour to try to flip the US House.

She popped into the famed West Coast eatery in Delano on Friday and emerged with a smile while gripping a red, white and yellow bag of grub with its iconic logo facing outward.

AOC stood in line inside the franchise with her arms crossed, then gave a quick wave to photographers waiting outside while she was being guarded by a security detail.

She satisfied her burger craving after stumping for about 15 minutes for lefty Democrat Randy Villegas, who is campaigning to unseat Rep. David Valadao (R-Ca.) in a heavily Hispanic district that Democrats redrew to their advantage after Republicans did the same in Texas and other states.

Valadao has taken steps to distance himself from President Trump in territory that Trump carried by just 2% against Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. The California incumbent voted to impeach the president in 2021, but backed his Big Beautiful Bill in 2025.

AOC will need sustenance for the road ahead, with plans to campaign in Las Vegas later Saturday, where she holds a Get out the Early Vote Rally along with Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.).

“The same forces rigging the economy against working people are betting we stay home this November. But the people who make Nevada work will never fold — we’re going all in!” Horsford’s campaign wrote.

AOC was recently all-in on another bit of regional fare on her recent trip to Michigan, where she made her first visit to a Culver’s alongside left wing Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. She ordered a ButterBurger and cheese curds at that fast casual restaurant, gushing afterward that, “My life has changed!”

She wasn’t so keen on In-N-Out back in 2022, during another hard-fought midterm cycle. Back then, Pod Save America podcaster Jon Lovett asked a blunt question about her take on “the quality of the fries.”

“Thank you for saying this because every time I come out here, everyone’s like: ‘Oh my god, In-N-Out, In-N-Out.’ And I’m like, my controversial, nonpolitical opinion is that it’s overrated,” she said. She added that her beef wasn’t with the burger, saying the joint has “dry fries.”
news.summary: Campaigning for lefty candidates all over the country sure does work up an appetite, as AOC proved when she stopped by an In-N-Out burger stand in California.

news.title: Mississippi's Senate Race Gets Close At The Exact Wrong Moment For Republicans
news.text:
JACKSON, Miss. — Scott Colom likes his odds.

“I think I’m gonna win. I really, truly believe I’m gonna win,” Colom told HuffPost over flash-fried Maine lobster tails and fried jumbo Gulf shrimp and fries at Johnny T’s Bistro & Blues. “Everything’s lined up at the right moment for me.”

It was unclear if Colom’s moment would ever come. Democrats, both nationally and in the state, had spent months insisting Mississippi was a sleeper race in the battle for the Senate, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) repeatedly telling donors to invest there. Colom was a strong candidate while his opponent, GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, is universally regarded as underwhelming; the state’s media markets were cheap enough for an easy investment.

But over those many months, there were few signs the race in a deep-red state with one of the nation’s most conservative electorates was actually close.

Until now. Both parties’ major Senate super PACs have put more than $1 million into the race in the past few days. Democratic surrogates, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, have descended on the state. President Donald Trump is set to campaign for Hyde-Smith on Monday. Suddenly, Colom becoming the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction is a live possibility.

He’s still a clear underdog: The Cook Political Report, one of the most prominent election forecasters, moved the race to “likely Republican” rather than grant it “lean” or “toss up” status. But the fact that Democrats believe Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney and father of two, could build on a series of stronger-than-usual campaigns in Mississippi and actually knock off Hyde-Smith in a state Trump won by 22 points is a vivid display of how far the president’s political standing has fallen and how ambitious Democrats have become in the run-up to the midterms.

Hyde-Smith’s campaign continued to project confidence as the race tightens, even as she welcomed Trump’s campaign stop. 

“Mississippians know her record: billions brought home for infrastructure and rural health care; conservative judges confirmed and liberal ones blocked; tax relief for working families and small businesses; a secure border; and votes that keep men out of girls’ sports and locker rooms,” said Jake Monssen, her campaign manager. “Scott Colom is bankrolled by the radical left because he is in lockstep with their agenda. He supports tax increases, open borders, taxpayer benefits for illegal immigrants, and sex change surgeries for minors.”

She has also so far declined to debate Colom, so the Democrat challenged Trump to a debate when he is in town on Monday.

“He promised the people of Mississippi ‘America First.’ He’s delivered ‘Mississippi Last,’” Colom said of Trump, hitting him on a series of broken promises. “You promised you’re going to look out for the farmers. Well, tariffs have been terrible. You promised no more endless wars. We’re back at war with no end in sight. You lied.”

He continued: “You betrayed your voters, and instead of looking out for them, you’re looking out for yourself. You made 2.2 billion dollars on a crypto scheme. You got a private jet for Qatar. How’s that benefiting Mississippians?”

“I want to debate him. I’m ready to go,” Colom declared giddily. 

Colom’s moment has been a long time coming. He said just four people showed up to the first town hall he held in Jackson during his campaign.

“And I just kept going,” he said. “I kept doing town halls, and people started to say, ‘Man, this guy is really out there. He’s really trying to listen to us. He’s going to the music festival. He’s going to the housing project. He’s actually showing up in a way that we haven’t seen in a long time.’”

Things began to shift, in Colom’s estimation, after his team released an ad skewering Hyde-Smith’s suggestion that voters pick other proteins at the grocery store due to the rising cost of beef. Colom’s ad shows voters opting to “pick another senator instead.”

The ad went viral, with over 2 million views on X.

“When I did the ad, I wasn’t thinking about the grandma that watched the news, right? I was thinking about the young person that doesn’t listen to politics, doesn’t pay attention to political ads. But how do I get that person’s attention? Do something edgy, something that feels different.”

And he’s had some reinforcements. Democrats like Pete Buttigieg, Cory Booker, and Raphael Warnock have joined Colom on the stump. Former President Barack Obama has backed his candidacy. On Thursday, Harris was up to bat, joining Colom for a rural roundtable and a rally in Columbus, near the Alabama border.

“We are on the verge of making a statement not only about who we are as Americans, who you are as Mississippians, but also the kind of future that we want for our children, for our families, for our parents and grandparents, for the ancestors that we honor. We are able right now to make a statement,” Harris said to a riled-up crowd peppered with many women adorned in her Alpha Kappa Alpha sorority’s pink and green.

She added: “Let’s take these next 12 days and do everything in our power, every minute and hour and moment we have, let’s remind people of their power. The power is with the people, and the people are with Scott.”

Colom is pitching himself as district attorney with a high conviction rate, a politician who is able to speak to voters across party lines. He’s praised Trump’s border policies and broken with Democrats on trans women’s participation in sports. Hyde-Smith’s team, instead, paints him as the preferred candidate of the far left.

But Colom doesn’t find campaigning with Harris — or other national Democrats for that matter — the third rail some may suppose this could be in such a red state. He thinks that presumption misunderstands voters, and that voters may begin to question why national Democrats are showing up in ways he believes Hyde-Smith is not. 

“The real question is, why does Senator Warnock care about healthcare and hospitals more than Cindy Hyde-Smith?” Colom asked. “That’s the real question. Why does Pete Buttigieg care more about these roads and bridges in Jackson than Senator Hyde-Smith?”

Glenn Antizzo, a history and political science professor at Mississippi Christian University, said Hyde-Smith does have political vulnerabilities: The “pick another protein” message highlights her propensity for gaffes, and she is liked less in the state than her senior counterpart, Roger Wicker.

“Mississippi tends to look at politics as a team sport in a way, and you know you may not like the players on your team, but you don’t hate them enough to want to see the other team win,” Antizzo added.

Democrats’ chances in the state have long been bedeviled by its intense racial polarization: While the state has the largest percentage of Black registered voters anywhere in the country, they are nonetheless outnumbered by conservative white voters.

But recent elections in the state have given Democrats hope they can finally solve the befuddling math of winning here: Former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy lost to Hyde-Smith in a 2018 runoff by just seven points, then former state Attorney General Jim Hood lost the 2019 governor’s race by just five points. Finally, Brenden Presley (yes, he’s related to Elvis) lost the governor’s race in 2023 by just 27,000 votes.

The increasing competitiveness of the state could continue into next year, when the governor’s race will be open. Colom told HuffPost he just doesn’t see, “under any circumstances,” a run for governor in the cards for him if he loses.

“God will really have to call me to do that,” he said. “I don’t see that happening. I don’t see that happening.”

There is the question, of course, of whether Colom’s moment is coming too late. State Rep. Zakiya Summers, who represents Jackson, said national Democrats needed to spend directly earlier on.

“We were disappointed that we did not get the level of support from some of the national, like the DNC and the other PACs,” said Summers, adding: “I think that it is a disservice to our state, and is a consequence that we aren’t putting money where we could actually have lasting, impactful change.”

But she’s not discouraged: “Maybe I’m being naive, but I’m gonna keep on this optimistic train that we’re going to show the world on November 3 what Mississippi can do ... and they will see that your dollars, when you invest in Mississippi, they don’t go to waste.”

news.title: AOC can draw a crowd. The midterms will test whether her politics can win before 2028
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has had little trouble drawing a crowd.

In a final campaign swing with progressive candidates across the country, the Democratic congresswoman from New York packed rooms in Michigan’s deeply Republican Upper Peninsula, where chants of “AOC” broke out.

In Ohio and Maine, hundreds of students turned out to catch a glimpse of her as she campaigned alongside Democrats in competitive races in the Nov. 3 midterms. On Friday night, she was in California’s Central Valley, lending support to a progressive seeking to unseat a House Republican.

Ocasio-Cortez has built a national following that few other members of Congress can match. Her tens of millions of social media followers give her a platform far beyond her New York district, and her nickname, AOC, has become one of the most recognizable in American politics.

Now, as she contemplates a next move, including a possible run for the White House or the Senate, she is also offering a largely untested proposition: that her brand of progressive politics can appeal beyond the Democratic base and help the party win those competitive elections.

“We have written a check on the left, saying if you champion these policies that have popular support, we can win,” Ocasio-Cortez told a recent fundraiser. “Now it is time to cash in. Now it is time to go out and show what we are capable of.”

At 37, she is the natural heir to the political movement fostered by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont that has had striking appeal for young voters. It also offers a stark contrast to the roles that the superrich like Elon Musk are trying to play in influencing elections.

“You have to be the right person at the right place at the right time,” said Doug Sosnik, who was a senior adviser to Democratic President Bill Clinton. “The year that Jimmy Carter ran and got elected president is the only year I think he could have run and gotten elected.”

The progressive brand is on the line in Maine and Michigan Senate races

In a historic concert hall in Portland, Maine, filled with college students, retirees and others, Ocasio-Cortez looked to Senate nominee Troy Jackson and acknowledged the political calculation of his appearance alongside her.

“There are a lot of consultants out here in Washington that would tell him, ‘Do not sit on a stage next to her,’” she said.

Minutes later, Ocasio-Cortez received rousing applause after an emphatic response to a question about putting “America first or Israel first.” She argued that the United States should question how it can afford wars rather than programs such as “Medicare for All.”

“Going back to her previous comment, why wouldn’t I want to sit alongside someone who just talked like that?” Jackson asked.

Maine, where Jackson is trying to defeat five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins, will be pivotal in determining which party controls the Senate. So will Michigan, where Ocasio-Cortez recently appeared with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Upper Peninsula.

In Iron Mountain, a town near the Wisconsin line in a county that President Donald Trump won by more than 30 percentage points, Ocasio-Cortez made the case for the progressive movement.

“Our problems are less left and right,” she said. “They’re top and bottom.”

Isabella Pruter, a junior at the University of Michigan, said Ocasio-Cortez has a certain star power among younger voters.

“I remember in 2020 and hearing about her name and thinking she was so cool,” Pruter said. “She really clicks with anyone who’s younger, especially for college students.”

At the New York fundraiser for El-Sayed this month, Ocasio-Cortez made clear how much she believes is at stake in Michigan. “If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” she said.

But not everyone agrees that enthusiasm for progressive candidates will translate into victories in competitive states.

Former Rep. Fred Upton, a Michigan Republican who retired from Congress after voting to impeach Trump in 2021, said winning swing states requires appealing beyond a party’s base to independent voters.

“There’s a place in the party for her but I don’t think it’s a majority,” said Upton, who served with Ocasio-Cortez. “She’ll win New York and California, but not in other states they’d need to get to 270” electoral votes to win the White House.

Heading west to help House candidates

The next stretch of Ocasio-Cortez’s swing took her west to gauge her appeal in closely contested House districts and spend time in a state important to a potential 2028 presidential run.

In California’s Central Valley on Friday night, she rallied with Randy Villegas, a young progressive who defeated a rival backed by Democratic Party leaders in the primary.

The race against Republican Rep. David Valadao is one of the most competitive in the country. The district is nearly 75% Hispanic, though Democrats have long struggled to turn out working-class Latino voters there.

On Saturday, she planned to campaign in Nevada, the second state on the 2028 political calendar and one that would be crucial to her path to the nomination. Nevada, where working-class Latinos are a major force in Democratic politics, has been friendly to her brand of progressivism and overwhelmingly backed Sanders in the 2020 caucuses.

She came to support Rep. Steven Horsford, a former chairman of the Congressional Black Caucus, near Las Vegas’ historic westside neighborhood, the cultural and historical heart of the city’s Black community.

A presidential run would require more than a theory of the case

Even if the progressive candidates Ocasio-Cortez is backing succeed on Election Day, a presidential run would present a different challenge.

South Carolina is first on the Democrats’ new early primary calendar, and Black voters make up a significant share of the state’s Democratic electorate. Sanders lost the state by wide margins in 2016 and 2020.

Jaime Harrison, a former chair of the Democratic National Committee and a South Carolina native, said Sanders’ struggles in the state were not because of his progressive politics, but because he did not put in the time needed to connect with voters.

To win South Carolina, Harrison said, “you better go to churches, you better go to union halls, you got to go to HBCUs” — historically Black colleges and universities.

“She has the talent,” Harrison said. “The question is, will you utilize that talent and focus it to do what is necessary to win on the biggest stage?”

At a rally in Columbus, Mississippi, that featured former Vice President Kamala Harris and Senate candidate Scott Colom, some voters waiting in line expressed interest in an Ocasio-Cortez presidential run, though they were not ready to commit their support.

Paula Small, a 58-year-old Democrat from Columbus, said she likes Ocasio-Cortez’s ideas but would need to learn more about her background.

“We are ready for a change. We are tired of the same politics,” Small said, adding that she believes it’s time for younger people with fresh ideas to get involved in politics.

Sosnik, the former Clinton adviser who considers himself more moderate than Ocasio-Cortez, called her an “unbelievable political talent” and described her as having at her fingertips “the zeitgeist of our times.”

But he questioned whether her appeal could extend beyond the Democratic primary electorate.

“I think she would be an extremely powerful force in the Democratic primary,” Sosnik said. “I’m skeptical that a majority of people in America would vote for her for president.”

Associated Press journalists Jonathan J. Cooper in Phoenix, Patrick Whittle in Portland, Maine, Mike Householder in Ann Arbor, Mich., and Sophia Bates in Columbus, Miss., contributed to this report.
news.author: Joey Cappelletti The Associated Press

news.title: California Post poll has signs of hope — except for third-place Gavin Newsom
news.text:
Steve Hilton is doing better than expected.

That’s the key takeaway from the statewide poll conducted by The California Post among 800 likely voters from Oct. 17 to 20.

The Republican candidate has run an energetic campaign, focused on ideas. And he did well in the debate earlier this month. 

He’s begun closing the gap — somewhat.

Hilton still trails Democrat Xavier Becerra by double digits. But he’s now within 16 points, trailing the Democrat 55.0% to 39.3%. That’s closer than the old RealClearPolitics average of 23.2%.

Hilton is also more well-liked than the Republican Party. He’s just barely underwater — 39.0% favorable to 42.5% unfavorable. His party, in contrast, only has a 37.1% favorable rating, versus a 59.0% unfavorable rating.

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

If Hilton falls short on Election Day, local Republicans may well wonder what might have been if the national party had put money and effort into helping him win.

The good news for Republicans is that California voters don’t like Democrats very much, either — they have a net positive approval rating of just 1.1%. 

Voters are equally divided over Becerra, and they have turned sour on incumbent Gov. Gavin Newsom. 

Only 47.2% of voters say Newsom is doing a good job; 50.4% disapprove of his job in office, perhaps reflecting his increasing focus on his presidential ambitions and his trips to early primary states. 

Newsom is leaving office at a low point. The poll shows that only 30.1% of voters believe California is on the right track, while 56.2% say it is on the wrong track. Worse, 44% of voters have thought about leaving the state altogether.

That’s Newsom’s legacy in California. Failure, disappointment, and pessimism about the future.

And it explains why Newsom is only running in third place in his home state.

Only 14.4% of Democratic voters in the poll said Newsom was their preferred presidential candidate, behind New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (18.4%) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (16.7%).

You have to be doing pretty badly in California to be losing to Buttigieg — a guy who disappeared from his job for two months without explanation in 2021, while cargo ships piled up at the ports.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, who has been hinting that she thinks she can run again, is doing even worse. She is the fifth choice for California Democrats, with 7.1% support. Her own party’s voters seem to think that Harris has had her chance, and failed, and should step aside for someone else to make a run.

The most interesting contests on the California ballot this year are the propositions. There are 14 of them. 

The most prominent are Proposition 39, which would require ID or a PIN number to vote; and Proposition 40, the “billionaire tax,” a one-time confiscation of 5% of the wealth of the state’s richest.

Proposition 39 is losing, but still has a chance, with 45.6% of likely voters supporting it, and 47.8% opposing it. A big effort from the Yes camp in the closing days could push voter ID across the finish line. 

Perhaps some California-style ballot harvesting would be useful in passing Proposition 39. After all, no ID is required (yet).

It’s not that voter ID is unpopular in California. But opponents have tied it to the Republican Party, and that’s enough for many voters in the Golden State to turn away. It’s possible that the recent, high-profile arrests of noncitizens for voting in California might convince voters to give ID a chance.

Proposition 40 is also struggling. A majority — 52.6% — of likely voters say that they oppose the “billionaire tax,” and only 34.5% support it. If accurate, that would be a profound reversal from earlier polls during the campaign. Evidently the sight of entrepreneurs leaving the state has had a sobering effect.

What these results also suggest is that while partisan loyalties remain strong in California, the electorate retains a streak of independence — the same streak that saw voters turn down affirmative action in 2020, the same year that they chose Joe Biden over Donald Trump by a 2-to-1 margin.

If the “billionaire tax” fails, proponents of Proposition 40 will look back with regret on their decision to make the tax retroactive to Jan. 1, 2026. That is what triggered the exodus of billionaires in late 2025, which instantly raised public awareness of the proposal — as well as of its staggering economic costs.

Overall, in a year when the electorate is hungry for change, the results of the poll suggest that what California voters are likely to get is the status quo instead.

Give Hilton credit for keeping things interesting, and changing some minds. His efforts may pay off one day. Given more time, and more money, he might have made the race more competitive. But perhaps not this November.

Joel Pollak is Opinion editor of the California Post.
news.summary: Steve Hilton is doing better than expected.
news.author: Joel Pollak

news.title: Kamala Harris returns to US campaign trail with midterms, 2028 in view
news.text:
Kamala Harris is returning to the campaign trail to help Democrats in some of the tightest US midterm races, putting the former vice president back before voters as she weighs whether to make a third run for the presidency in 2028.

The Democratic Party’s unsuccessful 2024 standard-bearer has made relatively few public appearances this year. But with her party trying to break the Republican hold on Congress on November 3, Harris is rallying in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, a return likely to renew questions about her political future as a crowded field of potential 2028 contenders takes shape.

Harris kicked off her tour in Las Vegas on Tuesday with a new stump speech attacking what she described as the cruelty of President Donald Trump, mixed with the aspirational aphorisms that have long been her calling card as the first Black and Asian person and first woman to become vice president.

She spoke to scores of Culinary Workers Union members alongside gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, Nevada’s first Black attorney general, who she said would be the “first Black governor west of the Mississippi.”

“We got a serious fight in front of us,” Harris said. “We are witnessing pure brutality come out of what is undoubtedly the most corrupt, callous and incompetent presidential administration.”

Like Trump, who is jetting around the country for Republican candidates, Harris is not broadly popular among voters. A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll in June showed 39% of Americans viewed her favorably, but the figures were starkly partisan: 82% of Democrats viewed her favorably, compared to 7% of Republicans and 33% of independents.

“At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters,” said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee. “That’s what’s going on here with her, and frankly with Trump.”

The day after Las Vegas, Harris led chants of “Mississippi matters!” to a crowd supporting Scott Colom in the city of Columbus. Colom is seeking to become the first Democratic US senator elected in Mississippi since 1982, and polls show an unusually tight race with Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Harris opened with advice she said she gives young people she mentors: “Never let someone else’s limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition,” she said. “Let me repeat that.” And she did, louder than the first time, drawing cheers from the crowd.

UNDECIDED ON 2028

If Harris decides to run again for the White House in 2028, she would likely be among the most high-profile names in what is expected to be a crowded Democratic field.

But Harris also carries the baggage of past defeats: she lost the 2024 presidential election to Trump, and her first White House campaign ended before the 2020 Democratic nominating contests began.

A 2028 campaign would also force Harris to revisit the Democrats’ chaotic 2024 race, when then-President Joe Biden abruptly ended his reelection campaign over questions about his health and mental acuity and she replaced him as the nominee.

Harris has since called Biden’s decision to seek reelection “reckless” in her memoir “107 Days,” a reference to the short campaign she inherited. This month, she offered her clearest criticism yet of his support for Israel’s war in Gaza, rebuking the Israeli government’s “horrific conduct” and saying the US should have “acted sooner and more forcefully.”

“All these things will be relitigated,” Kamarck said. “What happened to Biden? Did she know? Did she think he was losing it? And on and on and on.”

Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist and author of “How the Democrats Lost America,” said the party has tended to give short shrift to candidates who have lost, though voters disillusioned with Trump may also view Harris in a new light.

“She has that kind of crossover appeal,” Ferson said, “particularly with people who left in 2024 or stayed home.” Her implicit message, he suggested, is “Do you regret staying home?”

This month, as she wrapped up an appearance on the “Baby, This Is Keke Palmer” video podcast, Palmer asked her if she would run again.

“Oh, girl, come on!” Harris said, laughing while gripping the hands of the Hollywood movie star. “I haven’t decided yet.”

“But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms,” Harris went on. “2028 don’t matter if we don’t do 2026 right.”

news.title: This NSFW Cartoon Keeps Mocking Trump. There's A Reason He Can't Just Make It Stop.
news.text:
In the world of “South Park” ― where every episode of the NSFW cartoon is designed to shock, offend or provoke ― nothing and no one is off-limits. Not celebrities, not religious figures and certainly not politicians.

But few have been skewered as relentlessly as President Donald Trump.

“South Park” has a long history of poking fun at the president, one that began well before the show turned its attention to the chaos of his administration.

Before Trump became a recurring target in his own right, the series introduced a Trump-inspired version of Mr. Garrison, the schoolteacher-turned-presidential candidate, during Season 19 in 2015. After Trump rose to political prominence that year, Garrison took on an increasingly Trump-like persona, serving as the show’s stand-in for several seasons before being phased out after Season 26 in 2023.

But in his second term, Trump has once again become a regular target of “South Park’s” scathing humor, as the show takes aim at his leadership through relentless mockery and countless below-the-belt jokes (literally).

“South Park” hasn’t always focused on America’s political landscape. Since its 1997 debut, the animated provocateur — which typically follows the outrageous misadventures of elementary school friends Stan, Kyle, Cartman and Kenny in their small Colorado town — has made a name for itself with crude, violent and grotesque dark comedy.

Over the years, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have turned virtually everyone and everything in pop culture, and well beyond, into fodder for their unapologetic satire. Although the duo opted to skip the 2024 presidential election between Trump and then-Vice President Kamala Harris, telling Vanity Fair they were tired of making fun of the former, his return to the White House has seemingly given the foul-mouthed satirists plenty of fresh material to work with.

“South Park” returned with even more pointed jabs at the Trump administration.

When “South Park” returned for Seasons 27 and 28 last year, Trump quickly found himself back in the show’s crosshairs. No aspect of his presidency seemed off-limits, from his administration’s immigration crackdown and push to bring religion into public schools to his penchant for litigation. That included his $16 million settlement with Paramount Global, the parent company of “South Park,” over edits to a “60 Minutes” interview with Harris.

The dispute even made its way into the Season 27 premiere, in which Trump sues the town of South Park after residents object to Jesus Christ’s presence at the local elementary school.

“You guys saw what happened to CBS? Yeah, well, guess who owns CBS? Paramount,” Jesus Christ says in the episode’s climax. “Do you really want to end up like Colbert?”

The latter line refers to former “Late Show” host Stephen Colbert, whose long-running CBS program was abruptly canceled last summer, shortly after he called Paramount’s settlement with Trump a “big fat bribe.”

Other Trump critics have also faced repercussions for challenging the president’s administration. For instance, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, who has feuded with Trump for over a decade, said the president’s Federal Communications Commission repeatedly made threats last year over plans to interview Democratic state Rep. James Talarico on his show. The interview was ultimately moved to YouTube.

Kimmel also came close to suffering the same fate as Colbert, when ABC temporarily took his show off the air last year over remarks it described as “offensive and insensitive” regarding the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. In reality, Kimmel had condemned the killing while accusing MAGA supporters of “desperately trying to characterize this kid who murdered Charlie Kirk as anything other than one of them and doing everything they can to score political points from it.”

Meanwhile, “South Park” has somehow managed to avoid the same circumstances, as it continues to take on Trump with little consequence.

“South Park” doubled down on trolling Trump, even after the White House condemned it.

One possible reason for the show’s staying power is the $1.5 billion streaming deal creators Parker and Stone struck with Paramount just hours before “South Park” went scorched-earth on Trump last summer. The agreement not only cemented the series as one of television’s most valuable franchises, but also secured its future on Paramount’s Comedy Central through 2030, leaving plenty of room for more Trump takedowns in the years ahead.

The show’s massive audience, which includes a key segment of Trump’s base — young, white men — could also make it harder for the president to retaliate without alienating some of the very people he hopes to win over.

Still, that didn’t stop the White House from bashing “South Park” upon its return last year for mercilessly mocking Trump with small-penis jokes and depicting him in bed with Satan in the Season 27 premiere.

“This show hasn’t been relevant for over 20 years and is hanging on by a thread with uninspired ideas in a desperate attempt for attention. President Trump has delivered on more promises in just six months than any other president in our country’s history — and no fourth-rate show can derail President Trump’s hot streak,” the White House said in a statement to Rolling Stone. 

The criticism did little to slow the show’s momentum, however, as the Trump jokes continued throughout the rest of the season and even this year.

Ahead of the Sept. 16 premiere of Season 29, “South Park” jokingly announced it was changing its name to “South America,” a move “inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google,” Parker and Stone said. The joke clearly referenced Trump’s recent renaming of Lake Ontario as “Lake America” and the tech giants that bowed to his decision.

The show’s creators also took another swipe at their parent company, Paramount, ending their announcement with a thank-you to “a Skydance Capitulation” — a dig at the company’s efforts to pander to the Trump administration last year to secure approval for its merger.

Neither jab drew a response from Trump or the White House this time. Not even the show’s opening gag, which features a naked Trump flossing his “teeny tiny” penis with the U.S. flag.

Jokes about the president and his administration have since cooled off, but any new controversy or antics could still make their way into a “South Park” episode, one way or another.

At an Emmy For Your Consideration event in May, Parker and Stone revealed they had originally planned to devote just one episode to Trump last year. But the administration’s swift pushback prompted them to double down and take their satire even further.

“We laid into him so hard, and the thing became: ‘Well, who’s the bully now?’” Parker said, per The Hollywood Reporter. “It became this just totally juvenile joke of like, ‘We’re not gonna stop. We’re going to do it every single week.’”

Backlash from MAGA supporters and others urging the creators to “move on” from Trump jokes only seemed to fuel them even more. As Parker explained, “To me, that was the whole season, was that they kept reacting, and we were like, ‘Well, God damn it. All right, we’ll do it some more.’”

Even if “South Park” eventually pulls back from its Trump focus, its continued on-air run has already shown a resilience many of the president’s detractors have struggled to match amid his administration’s attacks. That defiance, however, comes as little surprise from Parker and Stone, who have long refused to play it safe with their boundary-pushing comedy.

“It was a bully mentality,” Stone said at their FYC event, adding that the duo would rather lose everything than compromise their creative freedom. “We don’t care. We don’t give a fuck. We say it all the time. We’re not irresponsible, but we’ll go back to Colorado. We don’t give a fuck.”
