APFormer US Vice President Kamala Harris hits five states for Democrats before midterms

Former US vice president Kamala Harris has returned to the campaign trail to support Democrats in some of the closest races ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Her return has renewed speculation over her political future as she weighs a possible third presidential bid in 2028.Harris, the Democratic Party's nominee in the 2024 presidential election, has maintained a relatively low public profile this year. Her latest campaign appearances across Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin come as Democrats seek to break the Republican grip on Congress.Also Read: Trump's diesel price relief efforts grow costlier as election nearsThe tour also puts Harris back in the political spotlight as potential contenders begin positioning themselves for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination. However, she has yet to decide whether to enter the race.Harris began her campaign tour in Las Vegas on Tuesday, delivering a speech that criticised President Donald Trump's administration while drawing on the motivational messaging that has featured prominently in her public appearances. She addressed members of the Culinary Workers Union alongside Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, the state's first Black attorney general.Live EventsAlso Read: US weighs lifting 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods to help Susan Collins win re-election: Report Harris described Ford as a potential history-maker, saying he would be the "first Black governor west of the Mississippi.""We got a serious fight in front of us," Harris said. "We are witnessing pure brutality come out of what is undoubtedly the most corrupt, callous and incompetent presidential administration."Her return to the campaign trail comes despite limited evidence of broad public support. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in June found that 39% of Americans viewed Harris favourably. The figure, however, varied sharply across political groups, with 82% of Democrats expressing a favourable opinion, compared with 7% of Republicans and 33% of independents."At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters," said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee. "That's what's going on here with her, and frankly with Trump."On Wednesday, Harris travelled to Columbus, Mississippi, where she campaigned for Scott Colom, a Democratic candidate seeking to become the state's first Democratic US senator elected since 1982. Colom is challenging Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in a contest that polling suggests could be unusually competitive.Addressing supporters, Harris urged young people not to let others' perceptions restrict their ambitions."Never let someone else's limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition," she said, repeating the line to louder cheers from the crowd.A potential presidential campaign in 2028 would place Harris among the most recognisable figures in what is expected to be a crowded Democratic primary field. But her previous electoral defeats could complicate another attempt to secure the party's nomination.Harris lost to Trump in the 2024 presidential election after replacing then-President Joe Biden as the Democratic nominee. Her earlier presidential campaign, launched for the 2020 election, ended before the party's nominating contests began.A fresh bid would also bring renewed scrutiny of the circumstances surrounding Biden's withdrawal from the 2024 race. Biden abandoned his reelection campaign amid concerns about his health and mental acuity, leaving Harris to take over as the party's nominee with just 107 days remaining before the election.In her memoir, 107 Days, Harris described Biden's decision to seek reelection as "reckless". She has also sharpened her criticism of his administration's approach to Israel's war in Gaza, recently condemning the Israeli government's "horrific conduct" and saying Washington should have "acted sooner and more forcefully."Kamarck said these issues would likely resurface if Harris sought the presidency again."All these things will be relitigated," Kamarck said. "What happened to Biden? Did she know? Did she think he was losing it? And on and on and on."Democratic strategist Scott Ferson, author of 'How the Democrats Lost America', said the party has historically been reluctant to rally behind candidates who have already lost presidential elections. However, he suggested that voters who have become disillusioned with Trump could reconsider Harris."She has that kind of crossover appeal," Ferson said, "particularly with people who left in 2024 or stayed home."Ferson said Harris's message could appeal to voters who either supported other candidates or did not vote in the previous presidential election, prompting them to reconsider their choices.Harris says 2026 comes firstHarris has continued to face questions about her political future during public appearances. On the video podcast 'Baby, This Is Keke Palmer' this month, actor Keke Palmer asked whether she intended to run for president again."Oh, girl, come on!" Harris said, laughing while gripping the hands of the Hollywood movie star. "I haven't decided yet."She then redirected attention to the upcoming midterm elections, emphasising that the party's immediate electoral prospects would take precedence over speculation about the next presidential race."But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms," Harris went on. "2028 don't matter if we don't do 2026 right."Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Troy Jackson's Closing Argument: 'A Vote For Susan Collins Is A Vote For Trump'
news.text:
A new ad from Troy Jackson’s campaign in Maine’s high-profile and heavily-contested battle with GOP Sen. Susan Collins focuses on control of the Senate, arguing her victory would empower President Donald Trump.

“It all comes down to Maine. It comes down to us. If we send Susan Collins back to Washington, Trump has a majority in the Senate,” the ad’s narrators, a collection of seemingly everyday Mainers, say at the start of the 30-second ad. “He’ll have total control again.” 

The ad’s clear intent: Staunch defections among Democrats and independents in the state’s Trump-loathing electorate.

The ad comes with less than two weeks before Election Day; Jackson, a onetime logger who rose to become Maine’s Senate president has a narrow lead in polling averages and most forecasters consider the race a toss-up, though elections guru Nate Silver’s model gives him a roughly 70% chance of victory. 

Emphasizing the stakes of Senate control could help Jackson win over voters who don’t approve of Trump and the GOP but are nonetheless won over by Collins’ record of relative moderation and power in Congress. A Washington Post survey released earlier this month found Jackson with a 50% to 46% lead, but with voters preferring Democrats control the Senate by a 55% to 42% margin. 

Democrats’ success in competing in redder states, including Iowa and Kansas, has opened up more possibilities for them to win control of the Senate while losing Maine. But victory in the state, which Vice President Kamala Harris won by seven percentage points, is still part of all of their most likely paths to 51 or more Senate seats.

The ad notes Collins has voted with Trump 96% of the time, and suggests sending her back to Washington would lead “to more cuts to health care, higher costs and more war.”

“We all know a vote for Susan Collins is a vote for Trump,” the ad concludes.
news.author: Kevin Robillard

news.title: What if Vivek Ramaswamy Ruins Everything—and I Mean Everything—for the GOP
news.text:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Surge, a politics newsletter steeling itself for the sheer number of D.C. adults planning to dress as “Jon Husted’s ass” for Halloween.

We’re almost there, reader. There are just 10 days until the midterms. After that, and after several years of litigation in Alaska, we may know who controls the Senate. This week, we look at Democrats’ still-awful favorability numbers and ask how much it matters amidst all this. Regrettably, Wedgewood polling is no longer able to survey this for us. Plus: Mississippi??

Let’s begin with this week’s signature unpleasantness.

What matters now: How far could the Vivek blast radius spread?

This keeps sounding like hyperbole in our head, but we can’t think of anything that tops it: Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad this week is the most odious advertisement we’ve ever seen. It doesn’t hit hard at some element of Democrat Amy Acton’s record. It doesn’t hit hard at some personal shortcoming. It’s not demagoguery stoking some broader prejudice among the electorate. It’s just inexplicable cruelty.

The ad features Acton’s birth mother, with whom Acton has been estranged since she was 12, calling her daughter a liar. The backstory, which you’re probably familiar with by now, is that Acton had accused her stepfather of molesting her between the ages of 9 and 12. Her stepfather would ultimately be indicted for rape, but the stepfather jumped bond and fled the state with Acton’s birth mother. This is as repulsive as people get, and Ramaswamy chose to feature this sinister person in a campaign ad. That, in turn, is as repulsive as campaigns get.

We are almost certain—not quite 100 percent, regrettably—that this will backfire on Ramaswamy, who apparently wasn’t doing all that great in his race if he chose this path. There’s an element of edgelord-iness among Republican staff and consultants who’ve come up in the Trump era, who’ve seen Trump’s ability to get away with acts of cruelty and believe the power of the dark arts is boundless. But not every candidate is Donald Trump—Ramaswamy, certainly, lacks any trace of charisma—and voters of all stripes generally don’t like ads in which someone is attacked over her history of being sexually abused as a child.

Should this backfire meaningfully, we’re interested in the fallout beyond just Ramaswamy’s own race.

This is, after all, the biggest political news story in the country less than weeks before an election. And if the ad moves numbers against Ramaswamy, how much of that spills over to the state’s all-important Senate race as well?

While the administration—both Donald Trump and J.D. Vance—are standing by Ramaswamy’s airing of the ad, most prominent Ohio Republicans are keeping their distance. Grandfatherly Gov. Mike DeWine said it was “wrong to run this ad” and urged Ramaswamy to take it down. Secretary of State Frank LaRose said he wouldn’t “run an ad like that.” Retired Ohio Republicans, like former Sen. Rob Portman and ex-Rep. Jim Renacci, trashed it. The latter tweeted that “the floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor.”

And then there’s Sen. Jon Husted, utilizing all the glute strength he can muster to fend off a challenge from Democratic ex-Sen. Sherrod Brown. While Husted is well cocooned by his handlers at this point, his campaign issued a statement in which Husted said he “would not have run that ad.”

It’s about the only ad that Husted won’t run. While it’s not the most-discussed Senate contest in national media, the Ohio Senate race is right up there with Texas’ as the most expensive in the country, rapidly closing in on half-a-billion dollars spent. It’s pivotal, as most if not all paths to a Democratic Senate majority run through Ohio.

So if Ramaswamy’s ad, aside from nuking his own campaign, were to bring Husted down another point or two? That could cost Husted the race, and Senate Republicans their majority. How karmically just it would be for so much of the blame to fall on Vivek Ramaswamy.

What to keep an eye on: Alaska funny business.

What’s going on in the Alaska Senate race? Beats us. Sure, there are polls showing Democrat Mary Peltola with an edge over GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan. But who knows if those are right? Alaska is a state of 27 people who all spend their day in the woods fighting with bears. No “big-city pollster” knows what these people are thinking.

But let’s presume the race is as close as all indications beyond polling—ad spending, Trump and Vance visits, etc.—suggest. And let’s say that Senate control hinges on Alaska. We feel the need, then, to adequately prepare you for the amount of focus that could be trained on Alaska after Election Day.

First of all, Alaska is a full 900 time zones behind the continental United States, so its counting won’t be done until late. It also has a ranked-choice voting system, meaning that if none of the four candidates on the ballot achieves a majority—likely—the state won’t tabulate final results until Nov. 18.

And then there’s another wrinkle.

One of the four candidates on the ballot is Dan J. Sullivan, not to be confused with Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The senator sued to get J. Sullivan off the ballot, calling him a frivolous spoiler intended to sow voter confusion, but the Alaska Supreme Court allowed both Dans to stay on. It’s worth noting, too, that Sen. Sullivan is clearly marked as the incumbent on the ballot.

Now the Trump Justice Department is stepping in. It filed a lawsuit this week in Alaska federal court seeking to block the state from certifying “any result that may be impacted by voter confusion” between the Dans “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.” In other words, the DOJ wants to block certification of the state’s Senate race if Sen. Sullivan … loses. It seems like a stretch to us. It smells like one of those things, though, that could hinge on whether it seems like a stretch to Brett Kavanaugh.

What you can safely and comfortably ignore (for now): Democrats’ unpopularity.

The New York Times released a smashing poll for Democrats this week that, if correct, would deliver them a wave similar to the 2008 election, when Democrats won the House popular vote by 10.6 points. In a subsequent analysis, though, the Times notes one warning sign within the data: “Today’s poll found that just 28 percent of voters said they were satisfied with the Democratic Party, compared with 36 percent who said the same of the Republican Party.”

It’s true that no one likes the dumb Democrats. Especially when surveyed about it: What are you supposed to say when asked by a pollster, “Are you satisfied with the Democratic Party?” Who responds “yes” to such a question?

We just don’t think this is that important in 2026.

One big reason is that much of the collapse in the Democratic Party’s image post-2024 has come from Democratic voters, who are disappointed with the party for blowing the 2024 election and for not doing enough to combat Trump. As the Times notes, “Many of those dissatisfied with the party are, in fact, Democrats themselves—43 percent of Democrats said they were dissatisfied with their own party.”

But guess what the vast majority of those dissatisfied Democrats are going to do in November? Rush to the polls to vote for Democrats, to protest a miserably unpopular Republican president.

For an analogous situation: After that 2008 Democratic wave, no one liked the Republican Party. They had 41 Senate seats and 178 House seats and were generally understood to be bums. They got angry and weird and organized the Tea Party and formed a cult around Fox News television host Glenn Beck. And then, in 2010, they won 63 House seats and six Senate seats—not because voters suddenly liked Republicans, but in protest of Democrats’ governance.

Republicans, of course, went on to lose the 2012 presidential election, and Democrats will have to find a way to improve their image in the next two years to avoid a similar fate. All of the criticisms they’re making of Trump—whether on the cost of living or immigration enforcement—are things they’ll need to develop coherent, winning policies around heading into 2028 amid vicious factional disputes. Not to mention, they’ll need to find the proper messenger for those policies. Anyhow, that’s a mess for later. For now, Democrats don’t need to be liked to win.

Diving deeper yet into the dumpster …

• [Googles “Jim Newell” “Surge” “Wedgewood”… phew …] The Surge never did and never would cite Wedgewood Polls, a fake polling outfit that was busted red-handed this week for making up numbers that may have skewed races, funding decisions, or betting markets. When caught, the outfit then tried to cover it up by deeming itself a “social experiment examining how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem.” Oh, it was just a cheeky term paper, was it? We’ll believe it when a fraud investigation is completed.

• Those who had the misfortune of following the 2014 midterms will remember when Republican candidates lumped a bunch of things in the news together en route to a blowout. It was the “ISIS terrorists are bringing Ebola across the border in caravans” election. Anyway, we thought of that this week while watching this ad from South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott, in support of Sen. Darline Graham. In the ad, Scott warns that Graham’s Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, will “hike taxes to bankroll her transgender agenda.” It’s just silly: The transgender agenda is cheap. It’s the mandatory abortions that will require tax hikes.

• An interesting one to follow in Maryland (go crabs!): A ballot question this November will loosen the state’s constitutional requirements for drawing congressional districts. In other words, it will make it easier for the state legislature to gerrymander away its remaining Republican representative, Rep. Andy Harris, in the next round of redistricting wars. But even in one of the bluest states in the country, in one of the bluest environments this century, it’s looking like an uphill climb: In a recent (non-Wedgewood) poll, the plan only had 25 percent support, with 53 percent opposing it. Then again, maybe Harris, who is unpleasant, will just lose on his own terms.

• All right, fine: Is the Mississippi Senate race a thing? This week, Senate Democrats’ super PAC announced an investment there to boost Democrat Scott Colom against GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, while former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned with Colom. Trump, meanwhile, will hold a rally for Hyde-Smith in Mississippi on Monday. So is it really in play? Oh, absolutely—Hyde-Smith was only up 4 in a recent Wedgewood poll!
news.summary: Sometimes bad things happen to bad people.
news.author: Jim Newell

news.title: How Democrats could win the House, how the GOP could hang on, and where to look for a wave
news.text: In 2024, America swung to the right, powering Donald Trump back to the White House with the popular vote behind him and his Republican Party winning majorities in both the House and Senate. Just two years later, the country appears to be shifting in the opposite direction. Midterm elections are almost always a referendum on the party in power in Washington, and Democrats hope to capitalize on deep voter dissatisfaction with the president’s job performance and what they’ve framed as a crisis of affordability that Republicans have done little to abate. The battle for the Senate, always more of an uphill climb for Democrats to win, appears close, with limited public polling showing tight contests in a number of key states. The House, however, appears to be Democrats’ to lose. Democrats could add anywhere from a handful of seats to several dozen to their count, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis of three different indicators of the national political environment. But it’s not impossible that Republicans could hang on — or at least, prevent the Democratic Party from running up the score — thanks to a friendlier map bolstered by Trump’s redistricting push. Most Republican-held seats are in districts Trump won by double digits in 2024, meaning Democrats will have to reach further into states and districts Trump won to make big gains. And while elections are more nationalized today than in the past, not every district will see its vote results shift perfectly in line with the national trend. The individual characteristics of a district, as well as what voters there care about, play an important role in determining a winner. The candidates themselves matter, too, and incumbency can still be a powerful advantage for those seeking re-election. Even so, looking ahead to how House control could play out on election night requires making an assumption about the size of the national partisan shift toward Democrats, and away from the baseline set by 2024. For our analysis, we examine three ways of estimating that shift: recent polling data, past vote patterns and special election results. If the polls are right Districts to watch: OH-9, FL-14, TX-28 The NBC News polling average currently shows that 52% of likely voters prefer that the U.S. House be controlled by the Democrats, and 43% prefer the Republicans to be in control. This 9-point gap also matches the preferences of all registered voters in the most recent NBC News Decision Desk poll. To turn this 9-point margin into a shift, we compare it to the national popular vote in 2024. Trump won the popular vote by 1.5 percentage points, meaning that a 9-point preference for the Democrats in 2026 translates to a 10.5-point shift from the 2024 results. There are 238 House districts that Trump lost or won by less than 10.5 points, meaning that a shift this size could result in the Democrats winning 238 seats, a slightly larger congressional majority than they did in the 2018 midterms at 235. Under this scenario, we would expect to see extremely close races in some of those Democratic-held districts that Republicans redrew since Trump’s re-election in an effort to create safe Republican seats. One example is Ohio’s 9th District, where Democrat Marcy Kaptur, the longest-serving woman in congressional history, is seeking re-election. Republicans have tried unsuccessfully to oust Kaptur for years, and her district was redrawn last year to be out of reach for even someone with her political survival skills. Trump would have won it in 2024 by 10.6 points. A national shift of 10.5 would give Kaptur at least a fighting chance to thwart her Republican opponents once again. Florida’s 14th District is another. Republicans redrew its lines so that Trump would have won it in 2024 by 10.5 points. If the national shift is 10.5 points, Rep. Kathy Castor, the Democratic incumbent, will have a chance to hold the seat. Finally, look at Rep. Henry Cuellar’s heavily Hispanic district along the U.S.-Mexico border, Texas’s 28th. Republicans redrew this formerly 7-point Trump district into a 10.4-point one in the hope of finally dethroning Cuellar, who has survived despite South Texas moving to the right, and despite being indicted on bribery and money laundering charges. (He was later pardoned by Trump.) Even though Republicans are excited about their candidate, Tano Tijerina, and have spent big to keep the seat competitive, the Decision Desk rates the race as lean Democratic. If the polls are underestimating Republicans Districts to watch: PA-10, VA-1 Given polling misses in recent elections, it is possible that polling is overstating popular support for the Democrats. If that’s true this year, the battle for the House looks more like a coin flip. Voter demographics in the most recent midterms, 2022, with then-President Joe Biden in the White House, favored Republicans, were older and whiter. If we take the demographic profiles of the most recent Decision Desk poll respondents and compare them with the typical composition of those 2022 voters, as we did for a recent polling analysis, that 9-point advantage for Democrats among registered voters shrinks to just a 4-point lead over the Republicans. Comparing this finding to the 2024 results suggests that, under this scenario, the national shift would be about 5.5 points toward the Democrats. A shift of this size still gives Democrats a razor-thin edge — 220 seats for the Democrats to the Republicans’ 215. A slim majority like this would match the pattern of the past three general elections, where neither party has come out of the election with a majority of more than nine seats. The GOP’s path to maintaining its majority would require a slightly narrower national shift toward the Democrats — about 4.5 points — or a few Republican candidates outrunning the national political headwinds by just enough to win some close races. In these instances, party control of Congress would come down to districts like Pennsylvania’s 10th District. Represented by Republican Scott Perry, it’s been a target of the Democratic Party for the past few elections, without success. In 2024, Trump won the district by 5.3 points, while Perry carried it by only 1.3 points. For the Republicans to hold the House, they would need Perry to outperform that national shift. Virginia’s 1st District could also be competitive in this scenario. Republican Rob Wittman won this seat by 12.8 points in 2024, but Trump carried it by just 4.9 points. (Had the Virginia Supreme Court not struck down state Democrats’ attempt to redraw the congressional map earlier this year, this district would have voted for then-Vice President Kamala Harris by 17 points.) The party that ends up controlling Congress in 2027 could come down to whether Wittman can beat the national trend like he did two years ago. And if Republicans can manage to hold both of these districts and others like them, the party would keep the House by a slim margin. If the special elections in 2025 and 2026 are a bellwether Districts to watch: NC-14, KY-6 Another way to estimate the possible size of November’s swing is to look at the partisan shifts in elections held in 2025 and 2026, ever since Trump took office. These races include the 2025 governor’s elections in New Jersey and Virginia, other high-profile statewide elections and several special elections for the U.S. House. Although Trump lost Virginia and New Jersey, the other recent elections have tended to occur in places that supported Trump in 2024. Averaging across all of these states and districts, Trump won them by an average of about 3.5 percentage points in 2024. In the 2025 and 2026 elections, however, those states and districts supported the Democratic candidate by an average of about 11 points. This amounts to a shift of 14.5 points in the Democrats’ favor. If the Democrats are able to shift the vote in every district by such a historically massive margin in 2026, they could win as many as 263 seats to the Republicans’ 172. That would be the largest majority that either party has held in the U.S. House since the 1990 midterm elections. Such a shift could put into play districts like Florida’s 27th District, represented by GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar. Republicans in Florida left this district nearly unchanged when they redrew the state’s congressional map, believing that a district that Trump won by 14.6 points would be out of reach for the Democrats. But it appears the race in this heavily Hispanic district is tightening, as polls show Latino voters nationwide turning against Trump and Republicans, with economic concerns weighing heavily on their minds. These voters were critical to Trump’s winning coalition in 2024, and indications that they are moving back toward Democrats are helping drive the party’s competitiveness in Republican-leaning, heavily-Hispanic districts in states like Texas, too. Salazar outran Trump’s win margin by nearly 6 percentage points in 2024, and her survival in the 2026 election may require a similarly strong overperformance. A 14.5-point national swing toward Democrats could also make North Carolina’s 14th District competitive. Republican Rep. Tim Moore’s district is one that North Carolina Republicans did not bother changing when redrawing their maps last year. Trump won the district by 15.1 points, and Moore himself won it in 2024 by 16.1 points. Another district to watch is Kentucky’s 6th District. This open Lexington-based seat has been held by Republican Andy Barr since 2013, and was carried by Trump in 2024 by 15.0 points. Barr is running for the U.S. Senate this year. Republican and Democratic-aligned groups are spending heavily here, reflecting the importance of the race, as Republican Ralph Alvarado faces off against Democrat Zach Dembo. The NBC News Decision Desk rates this race as lean Republican. In 2024, this district reported almost 90% of its votes by 8:40 p.m. ET. If Democrats are on track for a massive national shift, this district may provide one of the best pieces of early evidence. National trends don’t mean every district shifts the same amount To be sure, all of these scenarios assume that the partisan shift in 2026 will be the same in every district. This may be true on average, but some districts will have a larger shift than the national average and others will have a smaller one. Demographics of a specific district may play a role in the size of the shift. For example, if Hispanic voters shift more dramatically toward the Democratic Party than non-Hispanic voters, then districts with higher concentrations of Hispanic voters will vote more favorably for the Democrats than the underlying partisanship of the district would predict. Incumbency can also play a large role in causing a district to shift more or less than the national average. In 2024, the incumbent members of Congress outperformed their party’s presidential candidate by an average of 2.5 percentage points. This year, there are slightly more Democratic incumbents seeking re-election than Republican ones. This means that the Democratic Party as a whole stands to gain more from the benefits of incumbency compared with the Republican Party. On the other hand, there are more Republican incumbents who represent districts with an evenly divided underlying partisanship. For example, an “incumbency bump” matters a lot more to a Republican in a district Trump won by 5 points than to a Democrat in a district Harris won by 25 points. Finally, redistricting has also played a key role in this year’s midterms. By redrawing districts in several states, Republicans stand to win as many as 10 more seats than if the map remained unchanged after 2024. Redistricting impacts the role of incumbency, too. When the lines for a district are redrawn, incumbents are now fighting for the votes of people whom they’ve never represented, and who may be less familiar with their record. This tends to diminish the size of the incumbency advantage. Republican incumbents in Texas and other red states and Democratic incumbents in California must lean heavily on the “D” or “R” next to their name when they try to win the support of their new potential constituents.
news.author: John Lapinski,Stephen Pettigrew

news.title: Obama Tests His Midwest Magic With Michigan, Ohio Stops for El-Sayed, Brown
news.text: Former President Barack Obama returns to Michigan and Ohio on Saturday to test his enduring political pull in two crucial Rust Belt states where he won two decisive victories, entering the fray just 10 days before midterm elections that could determine control of the U.S. Senate. Obama is scheduled to campaign for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit before heading to Cleveland to rally alongside former Democratic Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown. The political landscape in both states has shifted significantly since Obama left office. Ohio has become a Republican stronghold, while Michigan has swung unpredictably, backing President Donald Trump in 2016, shifting to Joe Biden in 2020 and returning to Trump in 2024. While his party continues to face headwinds, Obama's personal popularity has largely weathered the polarization of the post-presidency era. He remains one of the most popular living former presidents in national polling, and a recent survey in Ohio found him to be the only prominent public figure in the state with a positive favorability rating. Even so, the Michigan stop introduces a delicate dynamic. El-Sayed has previously criticized the Obama administration for falling short of progressive expectations, forcing the candidate to navigate past remarks as the campaign enters its final stretch. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed's and Brown's campaign for comment Friday. Obama to Campaign in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed: What to Know The rally is set for 5 p.m. to 7:30 p.m., with the location not yet announced as of Friday afternoon. Joining Obama on stage will be El-Sayed and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor. The state party is pitching it as a push to bank early votes, with in-person early voting now open across Michigan. Obama last campaigned in Detroit in October 2024 for former Vice President Kamala Harris. Detroit is where El-Sayed has the most ground to make up. In the August primary, Representative Haley Stevens took about 51 percent of the Democratic vote in Wayne County to El-Sayed's 45 percent. More than three-quarters of Detroit residents are Black. Among Black voters in the city, El-Sayed won just 31 percent against Stevens, Bridge Michigan reported. Pro-Stevens ads during the primary featured Obama praising her. Since then, El-Sayed has leaned on a string of prominent Black Democrats. Harris held a roundtable on Black maternal healthcare with him in Detroit, and Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock is scheduled to campaign with him, along with several members of the Congressional Black Caucus. Whether Obama would get involved at all was an open question for a while. El-Sayed has called the Affordable Care Act an "incremental" policy. He and Obama talked in August, reportedly about pulling Michigan Democrats back together after a bitter primary. The older record surfaced once the rally was announced. Days after Obama beat Mitt Romney in 2012, El-Sayed wrote in the Huffington Post that the result was no victory for progressives. "It was the rock we chose over the hard place," he wrote. The column went after Obama's record on war, civil liberties and deportations. On NBC News' Meet the Press on October 11, host Kristen Welker asked the Senate hopeful about it. "I was younger, right, and I was angry about circumstances," El-Sayed said. He went on to cite the Trump years as a reason his view had softened, saying, "President Obama was handed a really difficult set of circumstances, and he did his best." He also said he and other Democrats running this year might push in different directions than Obama's administration did. Obama to Campaign in Cleveland for Sherrod Brown: What to Know Saturday will be Obama's first visit to Ohio since 2018. He will appear with Brown and Amy Acton, the party's nominee for governor, in an afternoon rally whose venue has not been released as of Friday afternoon. In a Brown endorsement video earlier this month, Obama put the stakes bluntly: "This race is going to be close. It could determine which party controls the Senate, and whether Ohioans can count on the people in Washington to be fighting for you.” Cuyahoga County, home to Cleveland, is still Democratic territory. Several of its neighbors along Lake Erie are not, having moved from Obama to Trump over the past three presidential elections. Obama's standing in Ohio is unusual for a politician of either party right now. Bowling Green State University's October poll of likely voters found Trump at -15 points, Vice President JD Vance at -7 and Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno at -17. Obama, at +7, was the only public official in positive territory. The poll, which surveyed 1,000 likely Ohio voters between September 29 and October 9, has a margin of error of 3.95 percentage points. The national picture looks similar. CNN's June survey had 57 percent of Americans viewing Obama favorably, against 34 percent for Trump and 30 percent for Biden. Democrats were nearly unanimous at 96 percent, and almost one in five Republicans also viewed him favorably. In YouGov's summer rankings Obama placed first among political figures, ahead of independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and former GOP California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger. Why Are the Michigan and Ohio Senate Races Important in the 2026 Midterms? Republicans control the Senate 53-47. Democrats would need to gain four seats for a majority, since Vance is the tiebreaker. Holding Michigan is close to a requirement for that math, and flipping Ohio would be one of the four. Michigan's seat is open in a state Trump carried by about 1.4 points two years ago since Democratic Senator Gary Peters is retiring, Former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee, came within fewer than 20,000 votes of beating Elissa Slotkin for the state's other Senate seat in 2024, and Republicans now have a shot at a seat Democrats have held since 1979. Ohio's race is a special election. Governor Mike DeWine appointed then-Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted to fill the seat Vance gave up for the vice presidency. Brown, who held a Senate seat for three terms, lost his reelection bid to Moreno in 2024 by slightly over 3.5 points. His lead this year runs against Ohio's decadelong rightward shift. Both parties are spending accordingly. An Ohio Capital Journal analysis pointed to visits this month from Trump, Vance and Obama, plus roughly $750 million in expected campaign spending, as signs the statewide races are truly competitive. Trump campaigned for Husted in Ohio earlier this month. Newsweek reached out to Rogers' and Husted's campaign for comment Friday. What Are the Latest Polls in the Michigan Senate Race Between Rogers and El-Sayed? El-Sayed led Rogers 50 percent to 48 percent in Marist University's survey of likely voters taken October 15 to 18. The newest poll in the race, from InsiderAdvantage on October 21 and 22, had El-Sayed up a single point, 47 to 46. He went into the candidates' final debate on October 21 up about 2.6 points in the RealClearPolitics average. Rogers' best recent number came from a poll his allies paid for. The Tyson Group, surveying for the Rogers-affiliated Alliance for a Better Future, found him ahead 46 percent to 44 percent in early October. Fox News' late-September poll, run by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company, gave El-Sayed a one-point edge (50 to 49 percent). What Are the Latest Polls in the Ohio Senate Race between Husted and Brown? An ActiVote poll shows Husted with 50.2 percent compared to Brown's 49.8 percent. The poll surveyed 400 likely midterm voters from September 26 to October 18, 2026, and had an average expected error of 4.9 percent. A Marist University poll shows Brown with 48 percent compared to Husted's 44 percent, while 2 percent said other, 4 percent were undecided and 1 percent did not respond. The poll surveyed 1,176 respondents from October 15-18, 2026, and had a margin of error of 4.5 percent for likely voters. A Fox News Poll released Wednesday also shows that Brown leads Husted 52 percent to 47 percent among likely voters and 2 percent don't know. The poll surveyed 1,592 likely voters from October 15 to October 19 and has a margin of error of 2 percent. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anthony Murray and Jason Lemon.
news.summary: Obama rallies for El-Sayed and Brown in Detroit and Cleveland, testing whether his pull in two states he won twice still holds.

news.title: The seven knife-edge races that hold the key to Trump's midterm defeat
news.text:
With the midterms just over a week away, Donald Trump is pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into last-minute ads and rallies in close-fought Senate races in seven seats: Texas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and Kansas.

Republican spending on Georgia and North Carolina has slowed in recent days, suggesting party strategists are losing faith in winning these races, though Trump has not given up and will be visiting both states.

If Democrats can hold the seats they have and flip four, they would gain control of the US Senate. Polling suggests that Democrats are favorites to win back the House of Representatives, where they need to flip three Republican seats to gain control. But as Trump’s popularity sinks – his approval rating is down to just 31 per cent in the latest Reuters poll – so the Senate map has looked increasingly competitive and Republicans are playing defence.

To be clear, it will be an uphill battle for Democrats to win the Senate. Opinion polls have a margin of error of 3 per cent, and if that margin favours Republicans, they could break Democrats’ hearts once again. And yet. Farmers have been walloped by rising diesel costs, which have soared because the US/Israeli strikes against Iran have led to less crude oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Fertiliser costs, tied to fuel, have also risen. Producing hay has become far more expensive and farmers, traditionally a bastion of support for Republicans, are financially stressed.

Trump declared at a rally in Kansas on Monday that his Agriculture Department would provide $8bn (£6bn) in economic aid to farmers across America hurt by high diesel prices – without saying why prices have increased. 

Trump’s campaign schedule offers the biggest clues to what Republicans are trying to achieve in the final frantic days. Republicans close to the campaign strategy say the President is focusing on rural America because internal polling shows soft support from men 55 and younger in these areas – the very same bloc which was crucial to Trump’s 2024 victory. At 80 years old, the President is criss-crossing the country trying to shore up support, even though he personally is not on the ballot, desperate to avoid becoming a lame duck President facing hearings and investigations from a Democrat-controlled Congress.

His campaigning is nothing if not energetic. This week alone, he has visited Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina and Iowa, with Georgia and Michigan this weekend to be followed by a return visit to Texas early next week.

Ah, Texas. This is the Senate race where Elon Musk is pouring tens of millions into trying to defeat Democratic candidate James Talarico, a young seminarian from the state legislature, who is in a toss-up race against Trump-backed controversial Republican state attorney-general Ken Paxton. The sprawling, oil rich state of more than 30 million people would be a prize indeed if Talarico could capture it.

A backlash amongst Hispanic voters against the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies could help Talarico. Yet Republican ads are hammering Talarico for his previous comments that God is non-binary, and that there are six genders. Talarico is focusing on rising prices and what he calls a corrupt system which separates the wealthy from the working people. Trump is leaning into Republican efforts to portray Talarico as weird and ultra-progressive. 

In ruby-red Kansas, a state Trump won by 16 per cent in 2024, Trump spent Monday night in the closing stretch of the midterm campaign warning that the US will “burn” like France if Democrats win. Why? Because opinion polls suggest that incumbent Republican senator Roger Marshall, who won by 11 per cent in 2020, is in the fight of his political life. A Midwestern rural state, in the heart of the Bible Belt, Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years. Yet Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, the pastor of a Methodist megachurch, is making headway by campaigning against Trump’s tariffs, rising gas and diesel prices, and what he calls the President’s “erratic leadership”.

In 2004, the journalist Thomas Frank wrote a seminal book called Whatever Happened to Kansas? How Conservatives Won the Heart of America, exploring why voters in his home state supported Republican candidates whose economic policies benefited the wealthy and not the working classes. Frank argued that Republicans used wedge issues like abortion and gun control to distract from their true agenda of tax cuts for the wealthy and corporate America.

In 2026, no amount of wedge issues can obscure the economic facts – Trump’s war with Iran and his tariffs have pushed up costs. Cultural issues still have resonance in conservative states, though. At the Kansas rally headlined by Trump, Marshall warned that his opponent Hamilton was “too woke” for the state because he supports gay pride marches – drawing boos from the crowd. 

Can cultural issues, which worked so well for Republicans in 2024 – remember the famous “Kamala Harris is for they/them, Trump is for you” ad – resonate more strongly than financial facts when Americans vote?

“You’re really sort of – I hate to say it – you’re sort of trending toward the purple,” the President told his supporters in Kansas on Monday as he stumped for Marshall. The governor of the state is a Democrat, after all. Can Kansas make political history by electing a Democrat to the Senate on 3 November or are Democrats’ hopes of taking Kansas and the Senate vastly inflated by flawed polls which can’t accurately measure Trump voters? 

Donald Trump is betting on the latter, and he’s defied the odds before.
news.author: Laura Trevelyan

news.title: The moment that saw Trump shatter JD Vance's dreams
news.text:
Vice President JD Vance has a big decision to make. As soon as the US midterm elections are over, the pressure will be on to declare his intention to replace his boss at the White House. An early foray into this minefield didn’t go well. In an interview with journalist Mike Halperin on Air Force Two, Vance said: “Look, I think if I run, the President will endorse me.”

You think? The President wasn’t having any of his cheek. Asked if Vance was right about this at a White House event, Donald Trump shook his head. “Well, I’ll tell you this,” he answered. “He’s a very talented person, he’s a very good person, but we’ve, literally, I don’t think we’ve ever talked about it.”

The camera panned to Vance, who was standing behind him looking embarrassed. “No sir,” he blushed. “I said that too.” Indeed, the Vice President had admitted in his interview with Halperin that he hadn’t discussed the matter with Trump. 

However, the President wasn’t finished yet. “It’s early, very early right now,” he added. “We have to get through the midterms, see how it goes.” Two days later, at a campaign rally in Iowa, Trump returned to one of his favourite topics – standing for a third presidential term himself.

“I think the law says that I’m not allowed to run again. I studied that phrase forever. Unfortunately, it’s quite concise. Well, the one thing that’s different, they cheated us on the second one, because we won it three times. So I think I have the right to run again,” he claimed. 

Trump can sound like a broken record about this, but he’s convinced himself he’s owed a third term. If Joe Biden could claim to be running for president right up to the wire in summer 2024, Trump is surely thinking: why can’t I pull off the same trick? If nothing else, toying with the idea of a third term and pursuing every (fruitless) legal avenue to secure it once the midterms are over would help to prevent him from becoming a lame-duck president. 

Whenever Trump is faced with an unpleasant decision or legal problem, he adopts the strategy of “delay, denigrate, deny”. He could spin the question of a third term well into the last two years of his presidency. But this would leave his Vice President in a tight spot. Evidence is mounting that Vance’s heart is not in becoming the next Kamala Harris.

In nearly 200 years, only one Vice President has succeeded in replacing their boss at the ballot box: George HW Bush, and he succeeded the popular Ronald Reagan. In contrast, Trump is historically underwater with voters, who disapprove of his performance according to the latest New York Times poll of polls.

The 41-year-old Vance has been sending out some bat squeaks of doubt about his future, at least as far as the next presidential contest is concerned. Asked at a CBS News town hall in Michigan whether there was a chance he might not run in 2028, he replied: “Of course there’s a chance.”

He added: “The way that I think about life, big life decisions – my wife will tell you this: I’m a procrastinator. I hate thinking about it.” For the first time, he admitted Usha might not be keen on remaining in the limelight. “We’ve got four little kids. My wife has never loved politics, she loves public service.”

There was a further sign of hesitation in his interview with Halperin. Although he sounded bullish about securing Trump’s endorsement, he admitted “no one has any idea what the hell is going on” as far as the midterm elections are concerned. A poor result, particularly in his home state of Ohio, could upend his plans. Solidly Republican since 2016, the Democrats are currently leading the polls for Ohio Senate and governor by three to four points.

Vance this week rallied behind his friend Vivek Ramaswamy, who is standing for governor, after the latter aired a despicable ad in which the mother of the Democratic candidate, Amy Acton, accused her daughter of being a liar. What the ad didn’t say was that Acton was removed from her mother’s custody after her stepfather was charged with raping her at the age of 12. That didn’t seem to bother Vance, who applauded the ad’s “audacity” and told disgusted Republicans to “stop whining about it”. 

It’s not just Vance’s lack of empathy that could turn off voters. He sometimes doubts his own campaigning skills. “Like sometimes you know media scrutiny, pressure, policy. I can be terrible at it, and that is the sort of thing that maybe you know, so I don’t know,” he told Halperin.

This week, a video went viral showing Vance being snubbed in the locker room of the Ohioan American football team, the Cincinnati Bengals. Only one player, Drew Sample, appeared to shake his hand as the rest of the players filed silently by. 

For Trump, who revels in all-American sports, this kind of incident leaves Vance with a big question mark over his prospects. Trump is never going to think anyone, least of all his Vice President, could be a better candidate than himself. You can count on him avoiding endorsing a successor for as long as he can get away with it. By the time he does, Vance may find that, like Harris in 2024, it has come too late.
news.author: Sarah Baxter

news.title: Mark Cuban says AI hack agents are like cockroaches, but can be controlled
news.text: Billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban said on Friday that he is "not a doomer" about artificial intelligence and that companies should be able to use the technology to protect themselves from AI-driven hacks by agents that he compared to cockroaches."It's like the cockroach thing, right? You build a new house, you get the guys to come out and spray... the one thing I don't want is cockroaches in my house ever. But the cockroaches find a way to get in because there's zillions of them, right? And then if there's one gets in, there's more that are going to get in, and that's kind of the way AI works," Cuban said, speaking at Reuters Total Health."It's all brute force acts, and if it's brute force on that side with the bad guys, you can also use brute force with the good guys," he said.Cuban, famous for his role on business reality show "Shark Tank" and his involvement in the Dallas Mavericks NBA team, ventured into healthcare when he started the online pharmacy Cost Plus Drug Company in 2022 with a standard pricing scheme: the cost it pays for the drug, plus 15%.In May, Cost Plus signed on with TrumpRx.gov, a website created by the Trump administration selling discounted weight-loss drugs.But the company has also moved into manufacturing. In 2025, it began making sterile injectable drugs typically used in hospitals in its own compounding manufacturing facility.Cuban said the company has built smaller, tractor-trailer-sized manufacturing facilities he calls "pods" that can be used separately or together to manufacture many kinds of drugs, including generics and treatments for rare diseases.He said the pods would eventually be Cost Plus Drugs' biggest business and would allow medicines to be manufactured closer to where they are needed in the event of a disaster, because they're portable.One holdup, Cuban said, has been getting regulators from the US Food and Drug Administration to sign off on the pods."We're talking to the FDA to try to get approval," he said without outlining the complications. "They're working hard to try to figure it out."Cuban campaigned for Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 and has supported Democratic candidate James Talarico for US Senate this year in Texas.He said two items he believes the US government should immediately put in place to help lower healthcare costs would be that all payments made out of pocket should count towards patients' deductibles and that taxpayer-funded health contracts should be public without redactions.Still, Cuban said he did not believe Democrats were necessarily better than Republicans on healthcare."None of them know what they're doing," he said.
news.summary: Cuban, famous for his role on business reality show "Shark Tank" and his involvement in the Dallas Mavericks NBA team, ventured into healthcare when he started the online pharmacy Cost Plus Drug Company in 2022 with a standard pricing scheme: the cost it pays for the drug, plus 15%.

news.title: Democrats' House of Cards Is Missing One Card
news.text:
Federal prosecutors unsealed an eight-count indictment Thursday against Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a Democrat, alleging she led a marijuana distribution and money laundering operation. Lucas answered on X: "I grew up under Jim Crow. I've seen what happens when people in power try to silence those who stand up to them." Her statement invoked history. The indictment alleges conduct, including that she used her post as chair of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to shield the operation.

The charges are allegations, and Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell said she is innocent until proven guilty. He's right. Lucas may beat the case, and she may even show the prosecution was political. That argument belongs in a courtroom, where evidence decides it, and a slogan can't stand in for the evidence.

I've watched this routine for years. A critic raises a fair question, and out comes the deck: the race card, the gender card, the fascist card. Every card gets played except one, and that one is accountability. Frank Underwood in House of Cards at least looked into the camera and told us what he was up to.

The tactic works because it ends the argument. Once a question gets labeled prejudice, nobody has to answer it. I've been deposed enough times as an expert witness to know that a claim is only as good as the evidence behind it. Real discrimination exists. That's exactly why the fakes do so much damage.

Consider Taral Patel, the Democrat candidate for Fort Bend County commissioner in Texas in 2024. He was accused of posting fake racist comments on his own pages, apparently to win sympathy. He was charged in September 2024, two months before he appeared on the ballot. In April 2025, he pleaded guilty to two misdemeanor counts of misrepresentation of identity by a candidate. A courtroom is where that kind of victimhood gets audited, and the auditors rarely work for the campaign.

Jussie Smollett got the same instant embrace. In 2019, then-Sen. Kamala Harris called his reported attack an "attempted modern-day lynching." Police then said he had staged it. Harris deserves credit for what came next. She said she was "sad, frustrated, and disappointed" and warned that false reports divert resources from serious investigations. Smollett was convicted in 2021 on five counts of disorderly conduct. The Illinois Supreme Court threw out that conviction in 2024 over a prosecutor's agreement, a ruling the special prosecutor said had "nothing to do with" Smollett's innocence.

Sometimes the evidence gets manufactured outright. In October 2021, a group in khakis and tiki torches posed outside a Glenn Youngkin rally in Virginia to evoke Charlottesville. The Lincoln Project admitted it staged the stunt. Staffers on Democrat Terry McAuliffe's campaign amplified the scene, one calling it "disgusting and disqualifying." 

Duke shows what a rush to accuse costs. In 2007 North Carolina's attorney general dropped every charge against three lacrosse players, citing a "tragic rush to accuse" by an overreaching district attorney. Cornell is the live version, and I'm not predicting its ending. A woman alleges in a lawsuit that seven fraternity members assaulted her. Hochul then handed the case to Attorney General Letitia James, who had posted that the woman's ordeal was "horrific and unacceptable." Two accused men now argue James prejudged them. No one has been charged. Both sides deserve a prosecutor who waits.

Then there's the case where the grievance was real and the first reaction still missed. Two federal juries found that Talonya Adams, a black policy adviser, was discriminated against when she was fired from the Arizona Senate in 2015, in retaliation for complaining that she was paid less than white male policy advisers. She won a $2.75 million verdict. Katie Hobbs was Senate minority leader at the time. Her campaign's first answer to the verdict pointed to a pay gap between Democrat and Republican staffers. Within weeks, Hobbs apologized, calling her response "shortsighted, unnecessarily defensive, and failed to meet the moment." The missing card can be found. It just took a verdict to find it.

Critics will say Republicans deflect too, and they're right. But a party that claims the moral high ground on discrimination should hold itself to a higher standard of proof when a claim falls apart, because every collapse costs it the benefit of the doubt it asks voters to extend.

The cost lands on real victims. Every staged attack makes the next true report a little harder to believe, a point Harris herself made in 2019. Marcus Aurelius put the rule plainly in his Meditations: "If it is not true, do not say it."

The fixes are dull, which is how you know they might work. Officials should wait for facts before they amplify an incident, and Harris's 2019 statement and Duke's collapse show the price of skipping that step. Prosecutors should enforce false-report laws the same way for every party and every cause. Parties should drop nominees and staffers who fabricate grievances instead of hoping voters forget by November. Newsrooms should label charges as allegations and run corrections as prominently as the original claim. And the rest of us should ask our own side the same question we ask theirs: what's the evidence? None of this requires a new law or a new agency. It requires the nerve to apply one standard to both teams.

Lucas will get her day in court, and the presumption of innocence applies to her as it would to anyone. Any youth coach knows the oldest rule on the sideline. You own the loss, then you study the film. A party that answers every question with a grievance card eventually has no credibility left to spend. The house of cards stands only until someone asks for the receipts.

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management. He writes about issues in finance, constitutional law, national security, human nature, and public policy.

news.title: Trump and the MAGA enthusiasm strategy
news.text:
“I took him from losing to being ahead,” Trump said of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is fighting for reelection not only against a strong bid from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola but also against what is essentially a Democratic dirty trick by a man named “Dan Sullivan” who registered as a Republican to run in hopes of pulling votes away from the real Sen. Sullivan. Trump couldn’t believe that on the Alaska ballot the real and the fake Dan Sullivan appeared indistinguishable.

As we discussed how Republicans can win, Trump pointed to GOP redistricting efforts to flip some Democratic seats. “We have the advantage of picking up some seats, right?” he said. He then asked “How many?” I said five, or maybe 10. Trump responded with “Eight? Nine?” All those numbers, including mine, were a little higher than some recent predictions that the GOP redistricting work will backfire, and Republicans will pick up seats in the low single digits. But who knows?

“I might be wrong,” Trump told me. “The country’s never done better. People feel good. The gasoline’s a little high, but it’s coming down. You know, gasoline is lower than it was with Biden and Obama, and I got rid of the nuclear threat.”

Trump’s critics will scoff at his “never done better” claim, and at least some of his supporters might wince. Indeed, one could make the alternative argument that Trump was elected to do one big thing — bring down inflation — and inflation on a yearly basis was 3% when Trump took office in January 2025, and it is 3.7% today. That’s nowhere near where it was — 9.1% — in the worst of the Joe Biden years, but Trump promised it would go down, and it hasn’t.

On the other hand, there is the bill of particulars Trump offered voters in Sioux City and every other place he has held rallies. Look at the stock market, he told the crowd in Iowa, and look at your 401(k). They’re both up. Then: “Income for hardworking Americans has soared to the highest level ever recorded.” That’s true. And then: “The poverty rate has just reached its best level in American history.” That’s true, too, referring to the period in which the rate has been recorded. Then Trump cited other improvements, in manufacturing and exports, some of which were overstated but did indeed reflect progress under Trump. In addition, for Iowa specifically, on Sept. 30 Trump announced the planned construction of a huge new steel plant in the state, which outgoing Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds called “transformational.”

“You just heard six statistics,” Trump told the crowd, resting his case. “Ladies and gentlemen, goodnight. I love Iowa very much. I’m leaving. How the hell can I beat it?” Trump jokingly started to walk offstage, his work done, while the audience cheered.

Say what you want, but that’s not nothing. At his rallies, Trump presents a compelling case for solid economic accomplishments — to go along with the higher energy and food prices that have made inflation so stubborn in the months after Trump started the war in Iran. He promises, of course, that gas prices will plunge as soon as the war ends, which he thinks will be after the midterm elections. That will be great if it happens, although until then prices will remain a real problem. Still, the good indicators in the economy are real.

So are Trump’s tax cuts. Onstage in Sioux City, he polled the crowd on their opinion of his moves to eliminate taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security. Reflecting the area’s economic and demographic makeup, no tax on tips was somewhat popular; no tax on overtime was more popular; and no tax on Social Security was really, really popular.

All of this, good and bad, factors into Trump’s job approval rating, which stands at 38.8% approval and 60.4% disapproval, according to the RealClearPolitics average of polls. A president’s job approval rating is one of the best predictors of his party’s midterm results, and Trump’s is, for Republicans, dangerously low.

I asked him about the job approval number. “It’s fake,” he quickly said. “It’s fake.” He pointed to the New York Times’s use of phony “Wedgewood” polls. That was a moment of real embarrassment for the paper, even though the New York Times said it did not use “Wedgewood” polls in calculating the president’s job approval rating. Nevertheless, Trump made the fake poll part of a larger indictment of polling. “The job approval, they said it’s 37, 38?” he asked incredulously. “I’m not at 38.”

I asked where he thought his approval rating actually stands. “I don’t believe I could be beaten by anybody,” Trump said. “I think that if I needed it, which I don’t, I think 60.”

What does that mean? Trump would say it means what he says — that his real job approval rating is 60%. I asked if he meant that he would be at 60 if he were running for office himself. “Yeah, I think I’d be in the 60s now,” he said. “Now, in the Republican Party, I’m way up. Show him the 99%. Have you seen it?”

By that last part, Trump was asking an aide to show me a video clip that he is fond of playing, of CNN’s Harry Enten, from Sept. 27, in which Enten said, “In the 2024 election versus Kamala Harris, [Trump] got 99% of the MAGA GOP vote. Perhaps surprisingly, I might have thought it would be 100%, but it was 99%. Compare that to his approval rating now with the MAGA GOP. It’s 98%.”

Put those numbers together with Trump’s experiences at his rallies, where he addresses large, enthusiastic crowds, and then add to that the persuasive fact that he has twice been elected president of the United States — add that all together and it accounts for Trump’s belief in his own popularity and ability to influence elections, even those in which he is not running.

I asked, “Do you ever think that you get such big, adoring crowds, and it’s almost like a bubble? Do you think, These 10,000 people, man, they love me, but the larger electorate, I’ve got to win their votes. I mean, there are independents out there?”

“I always cater to my base,” Trump said. “My base is big. I think my base is close to 100% of the Republican Party. … I think I’m close to 100. … It’s not MAGA, it’s just —.” At that moment, I interjected, “But it’s not the whole Republican Party.” Trump answered: “I think it’s close. I think the Bushes have largely faded. They’re gone.”

That’s certainly true. But the bottom line is that Trump sometimes views his Republican base as if it is the electorate as a whole. He draws impressive crowds made up of supporters who love him. He spends much of his time among people who revere him. Viewed from that perspective, a job approval rating of 38.8% just doesn’t make any sense.

If you start with Trump’s belief that economic indicators are strong for coming growth, and add his skepticism of polls, and then throw in his confidence in his sky-high, rock-solid approval ratings among his MAGA base — together, they add up to Trump’s belief that Republicans can win not just the Senate, which many observers see as too close to call right now, but the House, too, which those observers believe is lost to the GOP.

Trump knows the polls, of course. He is a close and discriminating reader of news stories. And he has certainly heard advisers, consultants, and others describe the adverse conditions Republicans face in races across the country. But what should he do? Tell his party that they’re going to lose? Trump knows how many Republicans look to him for leadership. If he appears to lose hope, they will, too. So he keeps at it as he nears the end of an extraordinary 32-day cross-country campaign tour. And he has a case to make.

news.title: What’s the Matter With Kansas (the Senate Race, That Is)?
news.text:
Republicans face a challenging situation as they enter the November midterms. President Trump has a historically low approval rating, and unless there’s a massive polling error, Democrats will regain control of the House. A Democratic landslide is taking shape as U.S. Senate races break for Democrats across the Midwest, and they look to do something they haven’t done in almost a century: win a federal Senate race in Kansas. 

In a surprising development, election forecaster Crystal Ball has moved several Senate races, including Kansas’s U.S. Senate race, from Leans Republican to Toss-Up. Incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall is squaring off against Adam Hamilton, a Democrat and former pastor of Kansas’s largest Methodist church. Senator Marshall holds a seat Republicans have held since 1919, the longest tenure for either party. But that seat is now at serious risk.

It is not uncommon for a president’s party to lose seats in a midterm election. Traditionally, they are referendums on the president and the political party in charge of Washington, and right now Republicans hold a narrow margin in both chambers. In 2024, President Trump defeated Vice President Kamala Harris in Kansas in a landslide with 57 percent of the vote.

Now, two years later, the president is underwater with voters in the Sunflower State, with a 45 percent approval rating according to Civiqs. The president recently stumped for Roger Marshall, calling him publicly “one of my favorite Senators.” A closer-than-expected Senate matchup has Senator Marshall walking a tightrope: distancing himself enough from the president’s unpopular policies with Kansans, but not so much that he isolates the voters he needs to win re-election.

“Loyalty to Washington is becoming a liability when voters are feeling the squeeze at home,” remarked political scientist Bob Beatty of Washburn University. “When a sitting Republican Senator in Kansas starts running away from their leader in the White House, the five-alarm bell is ringing for the entire party.” For the Marshall campaign, the bell is ringing loudly and clearly. 

A recent YouGov poll shows Hamilton beating Marshall by a modest 3-point margin, while a New York Times poll ties them at 45 percent each. However, the Emerson poll shows Hamilton up 2 points, 45 percent to 43 percent. Roger Marshall won his first Senate race in 2020 by beating Barbara Bollier in an 11-point blowout.

The key factor that made Kansas a competitive Senate race is farmers’ economic anxiety because of the state’s agriculture-based economy. Polling shows that voters blame the Iran War and the president’s tariffs for the high cost of living and the rise in diesel fuel prices. The American Automobile Association reported that last year the average price for a gallon of diesel was $3.62; now it is $6.32 per gallon, a 74 percent increase. Even regular gasoline has risen to $4.28, up 44 percent from the year before. (RELATED: Mr. President, Please Don’t Make the Diesel Price Problem Worse)

Fortunately, the Trump administration has worked to ease the hardship ranchers face. In August, the president acted to lower tariffs on imports of lean beef trimmings by 300,000 metric tons. Matt Teagarden, CEO of the Kansas Livestock Association, put it best when he said his organization prefers Washington to “let the market work.” (RELATED: America Has Been Enriched — Not Ripped Off — by Free Trade) 

Sure enough, Adam Hamilton presents a unique challenge for Kansas Republicans. In the 3rd quarter, he raised over $10 million more than Marshall and has crossover appeal as a popular minister and former Republican. His moderate stances on social issues give conservative voters a permission slip to vote for him and have earned him endorsements from former GOP governors Bill Graves and Mike Hayden.

Furthermore, Republicans are reading the tea leaves about Kansas and working hard to ensure there are no surprises on election day. The Marshall campaign has branded Hamilton as a “Chuck Schumer-funded Democrat” as the Schumer-aided Senate Majority PAC has $5 million in the Senate race.

In response, the Senate Leadership Fund, a PAC backed by Senate Republican leadership, has vowed to invest $14 million to help re-elect Senator Marshall. A large portion of that money is being redirected from North Carolina’s Senate race, which Senate Republicans consider a lost cause.

The Kansas GOP has a bit of good history: its Senate races have consistently defeated Democratic challengers. Since Senator Bob Dole’s close re-election victory in 1974 (Watergate scandal), every Republican Senate candidate has won by double digits. Betting markets on Kalshi and Polymarket give Senator Marshall a greater than 60 percent chance of winning re-election in November.

For decades, liberals like Thomas Frank have asked, “What’s the matter with Kansas?” as Republicans have dominated every federal election since the Roosevelt administration and liberal democrats have been left scratching their heads. The truth is, GOP culture has been historically ingrained in Kansas since the Civil War and has become a generational memory for Jayhawkers.

Now, circumstances have changed in the state and country, and democrats are competing for Kansas once again. A blue wave is coming to many parts of the country, but Adam Hamilton will need a Wizard of Oz– style tornado to beat Senator Roger Marshall.

news.title: 2026 Senate races to watch: where Democrats need 4 seats
news.text:
Control of the Senate in the 2026 midterms comes down to about seven states. Republicans hold the chamber 53-47, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats on Tuesday, November 3, to take a majority. A gain of three would leave a 50-50 split, and Vice President JD Vance would break ties for Republicans.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan forecaster, rates seven Senate races as toss-ups: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. Six of those seats are held by Republicans and one, Michigan, by Democrats, Forbes reported on October 23.

Here’s where the closest races stand ten days out, and what the national mood looks like.

The House decides investigations and subpoenas. The Senate decides who serves. It confirms federal judges, Cabinet secretaries and ambassadors, so a Democratic majority could block or slow President Donald Trump’s nominees for his final two years.

Most bills also need 60 votes to get past a Senate filibuster, so neither party would get a free hand with a narrow majority. Trump would keep his veto either way.

The House is a separate fight. Democrats need a net gain of three seats there, NBC News reports. We broke down the 10 House races that could decide control earlier this month.

Maine: Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson

Republican Susan Collins is seeking a sixth term in the only state with a competitive Senate race that Kamala Harris won in 2024, the Associated Press noted.

Her opponent changed midway through the year. Graham Platner won the Democratic primary in June, then withdrew in July after a sexual assault allegation, which he denies. Maine Democrats picked Troy Jackson, a former state Senate president, at a convention on July 25, ABC News reported.

Polls have stayed within a few points. Maine uses ranked-choice voting, so if no candidate wins a majority of first choices, the count can take several days.

Ohio: Jon Husted vs. Sherrod Brown

This is a special election for the seat Vance left to become vice president. Republican Gov. Mike DeWine appointed Jon Husted to it, and the winner serves until 2028.

Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his old Senate seat by about 3 points in 2024 while Trump carried Ohio by 11, is trying to come back. A CNN poll released October 8 had Brown ahead 49% to 43% among likely voters, Political Wire noted. Other recent polls have been closer. Ohio’s governor’s race has its own drama, as Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring Amy Acton’s mother showed.

Michigan: Mike Rogers vs. Abdul El-Sayed

Michigan is the one Democratic-held toss-up, an open seat after Democrat Gary Peters chose not to run again. Abdul El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit health director, won the Democratic primary in August. Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, narrowly lost Michigan’s 2024 Senate race.

A Marist poll released October 21 had El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48%, inside the margin of error, according to 270toWin’s poll tracker.

Kansas: Roger Marshall vs. Adam Hamilton

Kansas hasn’t had a Democratic senator since 1939. Cook moved Republican Roger Marshall’s race to toss-up on October 6.

His challenger, Adam Hamilton, is the pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, a Methodist megachurch in Leawood, and won an 11-candidate Democratic primary in August, KCUR reported.

Beyond Kansas, Cook also rates Republican Dan Sullivan’s Alaska seat and the open Republican seats in Iowa and Texas as toss-ups. A Democratic win in any of them would make a majority much easier to reach.

The races leaning one way

Three more states could still matter. On October 6, Cook moved North Carolina, an open Republican seat, to Likely Democratic, with former Gov. Roy Cooper running against Republican Michael Whatley. It moved New Hampshire, an open Democratic seat contested by Democrat Chris Pappas and Republican John E. Sununu, to Lean Democratic, The Hill reported.

In Georgia, Cook rates Democrat Jon Ossoff’s seat Likely Democratic, Axios reported.

What the national polls say

The national mood has been tough for Republicans. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published October 19 put Trump’s approval at 31% of US adults, the lowest of either of his terms, Al Jazeera reported. In the same poll, 47% of registered voters said they would back Democrats for Congress and 35% Republicans.

Prices sit at the center of it. In an Ipsos poll from August 28 to 31, 47% of registered voters called the cost of living the single most important factor in their vote, and 71% of US adults disapproved of Trump’s handling of it.

The war with Iran is the other big issue. Trump ordered strikes on Iran with Israel in February, and gasoline prices jumped. An AP-NORC poll taken October 8 to 12 found that about 8 in 10 registered voters want the next Congress to make lowering costs a top priority, and about 7 in 10 want it to prioritize ending the Iran conflict, according to the AP. Only about 2 in 10 said supporting Trump’s agenda should be a top priority.

National numbers don’t decide individual Senate races, though. Most of the toss-ups are in states Trump won comfortably in 2024.

When will we know who controls the Senate?

Polls close on the evening of November 3, and many races will be called that night. Close ones can take days, especially in states that count large numbers of mail ballots after Election Day, or in Maine if ranked-choice counting is needed. Many Democrats are also voting in person this year instead of by mail, which could change how quickly early leads shift.

Media projections aren’t official results. States certify their counts in the weeks after the vote. For a refresher on how the midterms work, see our guide to the House, Senate and what’s at stake.
news.summary: Republicans hold the Senate 53-47, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats on November 3. Seven races are rated toss-ups. Here's who is running in the closest ones, what the polls say and when results could come.
