news.title: Arizona man sentenced to prison for threats against Trump, Harris
news.text:
A Casa Grande man was sentenced to more than three years in federal prison after he threatened to assassinate then-presidential candidates Donald Trump and Kamala Harris during the 2024 election.

Rene Ortiz, 56, delivered a written threat to the federal courthouse in Phoenix on Election Day, Nov. 5, 2024, that stated, "execute the newly elected [President of the United States] by firing an M-16A2 service rifle with a magazine of 6 rounds,” according to a U.S. Attorney's Office news release.

The threat was directed at both former Vice President Harris and President Trump. But on Nov. 25, days after the election, Ortiz delivered a second threat to the federal courthouse in Tucson, according to the release.

In that threat, Ortiz said he would shoot “the incoming fraudulent elected [President of the United States] … at the inauguration on January 20th, 2025," the release stated.

When the U.S. Secret Service interviewed Ortiz about the threats, he repeated his intent to make the threats. He was subsequently arrested Jan. 17, 2025, and was convicted by a federal jury June 8 of two felony violations of making threats against successors to the presidency and one felony violation of making threats against former presidents, according to the release.

Ortiz was sentenced Oct. 20 to 38 months in prison by Senior U.S. District Judge Stephen M. McNamee.

news.title: Map Shows Where Top 2028 Democrats Are Campaigning Ahead of Midterms
news.text: Potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates like former Vice President Kamala Harris, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg are hitting the campaign trail in the final stretch of the 2026 midterm elections. Harris, who is seen as an early frontrunner in polling, campaigned in Mississippi this week and has planned stops in New Hampshire over the weekend. Ocasio-Cortez attended an event in Maine on Thursday, is in Bakersfield, California, on Friday, and will attend an early-voting rally in North Las Vegas, Nevada, on Saturday, while Buttigieg campaigns in Georgia. The campaign appearances come as Democrats hope to retake control of the House of Representatives and Senate in this year’s elections, as President Donald Trump’s declining approval rating fuels their optimism about a “blue wave” election. Democrats hope appearances by prominent national figures could build enthusiasm among their base, a critical goal in the midterms, when candidates are turning to efforts to motivate voters to head to the polls. But these campaign stops also give potential presidential candidates an opportunity to connect with primary voters ahead of the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and elevate their message and policies. Presidential hopefuls may also be working to build relationships with allies who could deliver important endorsements in the election. Although the first votes will not be cast for more than a year, potential candidates could begin announcing their campaigns soon after the midterms are over, and talk of the presidential primary has already begun. Where Are Potential 2028 Democratic Candidates Campaigning? Candidates are campaigning in several states with competitive races like Michigan and Georgia, but have also notably spent significant time in early voting states like South Carolina, Nevada and New Hampshire. Here is a look at where potential candidates are spending their time ahead of the midterms. Some candidates who have been floated as potential candidates, like Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, are up for reelection this year and have spent more time in their own states, rather than campaigning for other Democrats. Grant Davis Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek that the hope at this “late stage” is “not to persuade voters but to energize those already inclined to support a candidate and drive them to actually turnout.” “Each is trying to benefit off the other, and potential presidential candidates get the extra benefit of generating goodwill with the other candidate by helping them out,” he said. “That can assist them during the primary season. For the candidate being helped by the presidential hopeful, it can draw more attention to them, and help energize voters to actually turnout.” Newsweek reached out to Harris, Ocasio-Cortez, Newsom, Buttigieg, Kelly and Beshear for comment via email. Kamala Harris Harris has been making campaign stops in places like Mississippi, Nevada and Michigan. She is set to appear in Manchester and Portsmouth, New Hampshire, over the weekend, and is also set to appear in Wisconsin with Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley on Monday, October 26. “Mississippi matters,” Harris said during the rally in Columbus, Mississippi, with Senate candidate Scott Colom. “We’ve got work to do. We’ve got 12 days to make history.” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Ocasio-Cortez has spent her time rallying with progressive candidates in key contests like Troy Jackson in Maine’s Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race, Angie Nixon in Florida’s Senate race and Randy Villegas in California’s 22nd District. She has also campaigned with some of her colleagues, such as Representative Emilia Sykes in Ohio, and is set to campaign with Representative Steven Horsford in Nevada this weekend. She has also spent time in Western and Upstate New York. Some Democrats have also speculated that she could run for Senate in New York, rather than run for president, in 2028. Gavin Newsom Newsom has traveled to swing states like New Hampshire and North Carolina, but has also toured the South, visiting states like Alabama and South Carolina. Pete Buttigieg Buttigieg, the former Transportation Secretary during the Biden administration, has spent significant time on the campaign trail. This weekend, he is spending time in Atlanta, Georgia, to support Senator Jon Ossoff’s reelection. He wrote in a post to X on Friday, “It's time to get out the vote, Georgia! I hope you'll join Senator Jon Ossoff and me in Atlanta tomorrow afternoon. Together, we can get out the vote for Democrats up and down the ballot in the Peach State.” He has also spent time in New Hampshire and Michigan, where he campaigned with congressional candidate Sean McCann in Kalamazoo. Mark Kelly Senator Kelly of Arizona has been to numerous states including Georgia, Michigan and South Carolina. Most recently, he and other potential candidates appeared at IndyFest in Las Vegas this week, where he said he has not made a decision about whether he will run, reported The Nevada Independent. Andy Beshear Beshear, the governor of Kentucky, was also in attendance at IndyFest and said he did not have an “announcement today” about whether he will join the presidential race, according to The Nevada Independent. He will be spending the next few weeks campaigning in several states including Nevada, New Mexico, Georgia, Ohio, Wisconsin, Iowa, Kansas, and Oklahoma, according to a press release from the Democratic Governors Association. More details on those visits remained unclear. Where Is Donald Trump Campaigning? Democrats aren’t the only ones busy campaigning in the final stretch of the midterms. Trump has held numerous rallies in recent weeks. He rallied in Iowa on Thursday to support Senate candidate Ashley Hinson and gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who are both facing competitive races despite the conservative lean of the state. On Friday, he held a rally in Fort Myers, Florida. He is also rallying in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday and Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday. Next week, he is set to campaign in Corinth, Mississippi, Lubbock and Corpus Christi, Texas, and Chillicothe, Ohio. Democrats’ Chances of Taking House, Senate in Midterms Both the House and Senate are seen as competitive ahead of the midterms. On Friday, the Cook Political Report shifted 19 House races toward Democrats. It now gives Democrats an edge in 220 races and Republicans an advantage in 198 races. Seventeen others are toss-ups. Recent polling has given Democrats an advantage on the generic ballot. These polls can signal the mood of the electorate, but are not always entirely accurate and have overestimated Democrats in some recent cycles. The latest polling data from The New York Times and Siena University, conducted among 3,494 likely voters from October 12 to 19, showed Democrats up 11 points, 52 percent to 41 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.9 percentage points. If Democrats hold onto every seat they currently hold, including seats in Trump-won Georgia and Michigan, they must flip four seats to win it, as Vice President JD Vance would serve as the tiebreaker in a split chamber. They view GOP-held seats in Maine, which backed Harris by 7 points in 2024, and North Carolina, which Trump carried by 3 points, as top targets. On Friday, Kalshi gave Democrats a 91.4 percent chance of winning the House and a 67 percent chance in the Senate. Polymarket had Democrats’ chances of a House majority at 92 percent and gave them a 68 percent chance of winning the Senate. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Shapiro’s chances stood at 4.5 percent, followed by Beshear at 4.2 percent and Kelly at 3.5 percent. No other candidate had more than a 3 percent chance of winning the nomination. Newsom has said he would not run if Harris runs, telling CNN in September, “I wouldn’t run if she ran.” Harris has declined to rule out a potential run. “I might. I am thinking about it,” she told the Reverend Al Sharpton in April after he asked during the National Action Network’s annual convention if she planned to run for president in 2028. Harris noted that she “served for four years being a heartbeat away from the presidency of the United States.” “I spent countless hours in my West Wing office footsteps away from the Oval Office," she said. "I spent countless hours in the Oval Office and the Situation Room. I know what the job is, and I know what it requires.” Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in May in a conversation with David Axelrod, a former adviser to former President Barack Obama. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating." Ossoff has said he does not plan to run. “I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and frankly zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now,” he said on MS Now. news.title: Intel Democrats on how they'll react if Trump alleges election meddling
news.text:
The top Democrats on the House and Senate intelligence committees say they are preparing for the possibility that President Trump makes claims of foreign interference to challenge next month's midterm elections.

The lawmakers said recent intelligence assessments show no indication of foreign efforts to manipulate voting machinery or vote counts. But Mr. Trump and his allies have an established history of raising claims about voter fraud and election interference.

Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia and Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut said this week they have asked CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to be reachable by phone on Election Day, seeking direct access to the senior intelligence officials who could help verify, in real time, any claims of foreign interference made by the president or his administration.

"What we can demand is, what is the basis of this intelligence? What is the source of this intelligence?" Warner said.

"We're making the assumption that the president is not going to accept the results of what looks to be a very challenging election for him and his party," Himes told reporters on Wednesday. "There's a wide array of scenarios that we have war-gamed and trained for."

The lawmakers, who could become chairmen of their respective committees if Democrats win control of both chambers in November, said they are concerned Mr. Trump could cite fabricated or selectively presented intelligence to cast doubt on election results or justify extraordinary federal intervention, potentially including attempts to seize ballots or voting equipment.

Himes added, however, that recent meetings with career intelligence officials had given him confidence that analysts would resist pressure to manufacture evidence of foreign interference.

In a July prime-time address, Mr. Trump cited declassified intelligence about China's acquisition of American voter data to raise concerns about election security. The material he released did not show that Beijing had altered votes or election results, and it is not clear how much of the voter data acquired by China was publicly available, though the White House has said it included nonpublic data.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence told CBS News that Clayton, since his confirmation in July, "has made it clear to the leadership of the House Intelligence Committee and Senate Select Committee on Intelligence that he is available to them 24/7 on any issue."

A CIA spokesperson said: "Director Ratcliffe is responsive to CIA's Oversight Committees and will continue to be available as appropriate."

CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.

The lawmakers' preparations come as the intelligence community continues to track foreign influence operations aimed at American voters, but to date has identified no evidence of plans to interfere with the mechanics of the election, Warner and Himes said.

The intelligence community distinguishes between foreign influence, which is aimed at swaying voters or undermining confidence in elections, and interference, which involves targeting the technical aspects of voting, including voting machines and registration systems.

"Nothing out there suggests that there is either the capability or the intent to do interference," Himes said, contrasting that assessment with a "pretty robust influence environment."

He said recent intelligence assessments had observed influence efforts underway by Russia, Iran and China, with a "grab bag" of other actors, including North Korea, weighing potential action.

Warner said Russia was pursuing operations this cycle "similar to prior occasions," including efforts targeting Democrats. Himes added that Russian campaigns "are also particularly focused in a bipartisan way on people and things that have been aggressive on Ukraine."

Iranian actors are "looking at disruption in Europe," Warner said, while Chinese operations have been more selective and aimed at local races.

Ahead of the 2024 election, U.S. intelligence officials assessed that Moscow favored Mr. Trump's candidacy, while Tehran favored his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris. Iranian operatives were also accused of targeting presidential campaigns through cyber operations, including the compromise of Mr. Trump's campaign.

The U.S. intelligence community also found that Russia tried to influence the 2020 election to support the Trump campaign, while Iran sought to denigrate the Trump campaign. Intelligence agencies found "no indications that any foreign actor attempted to alter any technical aspect of the voting process," including voter registration or vote-counting.

Warner and Himes said Congress has yet to receive several election-related intelligence assessments required by law, including reports due 120, 60 and 30 days before Election Day. The committees received a classified update this week, and the House panel expects another bipartisan briefing next week.

They blamed the overdue updates on the tenures of Clayton's predecessors at ODNI — Tulsi Gabbard and Bill Pulte, who held the role in an acting capacity.

"The previous two DNIs had zero interest in complying with the law here," Warner said, while acknowledging that Clayton had made an effort to address some of the deficiencies.

The lawmakers also expressed concern about what they described as a weakening of the federal government's capacity to detect and counter election threats, with reductions to the Foreign Malign Influence Center at ODNI, as well as a significant staffing reduction at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which helps state and local officials protect election infrastructure.

Himes warned that the loss of technical expertise could undermine the government's ability to detect foreign threats, even if career intelligence analysts remain committed to producing objective assessments.

"You can do a lot of work with loyal analysts at ODNI or at CIA," Himes said. "If you don't have the technical talent to identify technical — either collection or exploitation — you have a huge problem."

news.title: Outrage as serial rapist Max Factor heir is sprung from prison early... but is banned for life from California town where he preyed on women
news.text:
Disgraced Max Factor heir Andrew Luster has been banned for life from the California county where he carried out multiple rapes in the late 90s, the Daily Mail has exclusively learned.

Pervert Luster, now 62, was sprung from prison last week and is living in a modest $700,000 bungalow in the small city of Glendora – 25 miles east of downtown Los Angeles.

But while the serial predator has been cut loose, the Daily Mail has learned that his freedom has come with severe conditions, including three years on parole, a life ban from Ventura County and an ankle monitor that has to be worn 24 hours a day.

He is also banned from coming within 35 miles of the homes of the women he raped – meaning he now lives on the eastern side of LA County, well away from Ventura and Santa Barbara counties where some of the women still live.

Luster was convicted in absentia on 86 counts of rape in January 2003 after fleeing to Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, having been charged with drugging and raping three women – all of which he filmed for his own gratification.

He was famously dragged back to California by Duane ‘Dog the Bounty Hunter’ Chapman in June the same year and handed a 124-year sentence for his crimes.

But in April 2013, Ventura County judge Kathryne Stoltz slashed his prison term to just 50 years on a legal technicality, saying the original judge failed to state specific reasons for handing him consecutive prison terms.

Then, in 2016, came Proposition 57 – a rule change championed by then Governor Jerry Brown and then attorney general Kamala Harris, which mandated that non-violent offenders should serve just half of their prison sentence.

Despite being a convicted serial rapist, Luster was added to the non-violent category due to his victims being unconscious during the attacks, which led directly to his release after serving just 20 years last week.

According to sources, city officials in Glendora had no idea Luster would be let loose in their community – only finding out about his post-prison plans when he appeared at the local LA County Sheriff’s office to be photographed for his mugshot.

That mugshot, showing him with a lined face and a head of gray hair, appears on the California sex offenders’ registry along with his home address.

But that was not enough to prevent outrage in the community where he now lives.

People living on the Glendora street where Luster has taken up residence said they were furious about the move, with one young mom-of-one saying she had made a series of desperate calls to the local mayor and to California governor Gavin Newsom to get him removed.

Glendora’s non-partisan mayor David Fredendall issued a furious statement after learning of Luster’s new home, declaring himself ‘outraged’.

He said: ‘The City of Glendora is beyond disappointed. We are outraged. Andrew Luster was convicted of 86 felony counts stemming from the drugging and sexual assault of unconscious women.

‘He was originally sentenced to 124 years in prison. He has now been released from State prison and is reportedly residing in our community. This is unacceptable.’

He went on to slam Proposition 57 – which led to Luster’s release – saying the city of Glendora had consistently opposed the measure and pointed out that supporters had insisted at the time that it wouldn’t lead to the sex beast's exit from prison.

Fredendall added: ‘The people of Glendora should not have to worry about their safety because of a decision by the State that allows an individual with a history of rape and violence to now live in close proximity to schools, parks, playgrounds, churches, and community centers.

‘They deserve better than explanations that hide behind the mechanics of a deeply flawed system.

‘We are demanding answers from Sacramento. We expect transparency regarding the circumstances of this release, the conditions imposed, and the measures being taken to protect Glendora residents and surrounding communities.

‘The victims deserve better. The people of Glendora deserve better. California must do better.’

Also furious at the decision to release Luster was California State Assembly member Blanca Rubio, a Democrat whose district includes Glendora.

Rubio, with Republican counterpart Marie Alvarado-Gil, co-sponsored a bill called SB 268 that was deliberately designed to halt the early release of criminals like Luster by adding the rape of an unconscious person to California’s list of violent crimes – albeit too late to halt the now bankrupt Max Factor heir’s release.

In a statement released on hearing of Luster being sprung, she described it as ‘disgusting’ and vowed to protect Glendora residents.

She said: ‘The recent news of the parole granted to convicted rapist, Andrew Luster is disgusting and unacceptable.

‘I am working closely with local officials and law enforcement to stay informed about the circumstances of Luster’s release, the conditions of his parole, and the measures being taken to protect the residents of Glendora and surrounding communities. ‘

news.title: California Democratic Primary Poll Shows Voters Favor Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
news.text:
California voters have identified their early favorites for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, and Gov. Gavin Newsom is not among the top two, according to a new California Post poll.

When asked whom they would support if the Democratic primary were held today, Golden State voters placed a Democrat from the East Coast at the top of the field.

Newsom, meanwhile, received only lukewarm marks for his performance as governor and finished third in the hypothetical primary matchup.

New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez led the survey with 18% support. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg followed closely at 17%.

Newsom drew 14% support. Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly was backed by 10% of respondents, while former Vice President Kamala Harris — who previously represented California as a senator and served as the state’s attorney general — placed fifth with 7%.

McLaughlin & Associates conducted the statewide survey among 800 California voters from Oct. 17 through Oct. 20. The poll has a margin of error of 3.4 percentage points, and 419 respondents answered the Democratic primary question.

“Both Newsom and Harris have not locked up the — what would you call — the progressive or the very liberal vote,” McLaughlin said in an interview. “They’ve got stiff competition for it from AOC and from Buttigieg.”

He added that candidates also need to build a strong demographic coalition, noting that minority voters — including Hispanic, Black and Asian voters, as well as women — make up a significant share of the Democratic primary electorate.

Ocasio-Cortez was particularly dominant among self-identified liberal voters. She received support from 25% of those who described themselves as liberal and 41% of those who identified as very liberal.

California voters offered a mixed assessment of Newsom’s job performance: 47% approved, while 50% disapproved. That included 41% who expressed strong disapproval. Independent voters were especially critical, with 62% saying they disapproved of the governor’s performance.

Fifty-six percent of respondents said California was headed in the wrong direction. Economic concerns — including the cost of living, the state budget, taxes, housing and health care — were the dominant reasons for that pessimistic view.

The poll presented voters with a list of figures frequently mentioned as possible 2028 presidential contenders, including Ocasio-Cortez, Buttigieg, Newsom, Kelly and Harris.

The list also included Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who each received 3%; New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, at 2%; former Ambassador Rahm Emanuel, at 1%; and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, also at 1%. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Colorado Gov. Jared Polis and commentator Stephen A. Smith were included as choices but received no support.

Another 23% of respondents remained undecided.

Jeff Jenkins, a provost professor of public policy, political science and law at the University of Southern California, cautioned that it is still extremely early to draw firm conclusions from 2028 presidential polling. With so much likely to change before the election, he said the surveys offer only limited insight at this stage.

“That said, I think it is interesting that Newsom in particular isn’t doing better — because if polls are tracking anything right now, it would be name recognition,” Jenkins said.

“That doesn’t bode well for him. By contrast, I think few see Harris as a serious candidate, so I’m not surprised by her tally,” he added.

The California Post findings are broadly consistent with other recent surveys showing that enthusiasm for potential presidential campaigns by Newsom and Harris may be fading in their home state.

A September survey from the UC Berkeley Citrin Center and POLITICO found that 37% of California Democrats were excited about a Newsom campaign, compared with 28% who said the same about Harris. Those figures marked a notable decline from March, when more than 40% of California voters expressed enthusiasm for each candidate to run.

National polling has produced a somewhat different picture. Three surveys conducted in October showed Harris leading the potential Democratic field with between 20% and 30% support. Newsom ranked second in each poll, attracting roughly 15%.

“They have national name ID, many of these other candidates don’t,” McLaughlin said. 

Both California Democrats have been making the rounds in key primary states to not only campaign for Democrat politicians but also market themselves to a more national audience. Newsom and Harris have openly acknowledged they are considering White House runs.

Most recently, the governor was in New Hampshire, while Harris will reportedly be in Wisconsin and Georgia later this month. 

The Post reached out to offices for both Newsom and Harris for comment.

news.title: Startling shift revealed among low-information voters who helped put Trump back in office
news.text:
The voters who know the least about politics, many of whom helped power Donald Trump’s 2024 win, have moved away from him and toward Democrats faster than their better-informed peers, according to analysis by pollster G. Elliott Morris.

Trump’s worsening problems with other key voting blocs that powered him back to the White House, including nonwhite men and younger people, have been well documented. Morris’s findings point to another group drifting away: low-information voters.

Morris’s October Strength In Numbers/Verasight poll surveyed 2,028 adults from Oct. 13-19. Two quiz questions asked which party holds the most seats in the House and in the Senate.

Respondents who missed at least one were labeled “low-knowledge.” That’s roughly three in 10 adults, and a quarter of 2024 Trump voters.

Low-knowledge voters, who backed Trump by 8 points in 2024, now give him a net approval rating of -27, a 35-point drop by Morris’s math. High-knowledge voters, who narrowly backed Kamala Harris, give him -24, a 23-point drop.

The difference carries over to the House race. Low-knowledge voters went from favoring Trump by 8 to favoring Democrats by 12, nearly triple the swing among high-knowledge voters. Among 2024 Trump voters, 18% of low-knowledge respondents plan to vote for Democrats for the House, compared with 6% of high-knowledge respondents.

They’re also much less enthusiastic about his signature issues. Low-knowledge Trump voters rate his handling of immigration at +34, against +74 for better-informed Trump voters, and they disapprove of his handling of prices.

Morris says the least-informed voters switch parties most easily, and likely backed Trump out of frustration with prices, not MAGA ideology. If Democrats don’t deliver, he warns, those voters could swing back.

news.title: Politico Poll Finds Impeaching Trump Again May Boost His Popularity
news.text:
Most people think Democrats will impeach President Donald Trump again if they win on November 3, even though the past two impeachments were ineffectual - and more think it’ll increase Trump’s popularity than believe it’ll make him less popular, a new Politico poll reveals.

What’s more, just as many of those planning to vote Democrat on Nov. 3 say their candidates should conceal their plans to impeach Trump - if it’ll help them win - as say they should admit they’ll impeach, even if it hurts their campaigns.

In a national poll of U.S. adults conducted October 16-19, Politico asked a series of questions regarding a potential third impeachment of Trump by Democrats, if they gain control of the House in the midterm elections.

More than two-thirds (69%) of adults said that it’s likely that Democrats will try to impeach Trump if they win the House, including 41% who say it’s “very likely.” That belief is even stronger among those who voted for either Trump (77%) or Democrat Kamala Harris (75%) in the 2024 presidential election. Meanwhile, half (50%) of those who didn’t vote deemed impeachment likely.

Only 18% called it unlikely that a Democrat-majority House would try to impeach Trump, while 13% replied that they “don’t know.”

Ironically, more U.S. adults said Democrats’ third impeachment of Trump would make him more popular (24%) than said it would hurt his popularity (18%). Another 34% said it wouldn’t have an effect, while 24% didn’t know.

The plurality’s belief that another impeachment would boost, not hurt, Trump’s popularity increases with the age, from a virtual tie of 18%-17% among those age 18-24 to a two-to-one advantage (30%-15%) among those 65 and over.

Additionally, only one in four U.S. adults said the previous two impeachments of Trump made a difference.

Fully 56% reported that the first and second impeachments “had no real impact on Donald Trump and his agenda,” including 62% of Trump voters and 64% of Harris voters - more than twice the number who said they did have an impact.

Similar percentages of all U.S. adults (24%), Trump voters (26%) and Harris voters (26%) said they think the last two impeachments had an impact.

Notably, winning is more important than honesty for many of those who plan to vote for Democrats in next month’s midterms.

Politico asked whether Democrat candidates should admit to voters that they intend to impeach Trump, even if doing so would hurt their prospects of winning, or hide their plans from the public in order to win.

As it turns out, those advocating deceit ended up in a virtual tie with those who supporting transparency:

“The Democratic candidate should say they plan to impeach Donald Trump, even if that makes it harder to win the election”: 43%“The Democratic candidate should avoid saying they plan to impeach Donald Trump if it helps win the election, even if that means not making their view clear on the matter”: 41%“Don’t know”: 15%

Young Democrat voters (18-24) largely favored openness over deception, 52%-37%. Results were reversed for the oldest (65+), with obfuscation topping honesty, 53%-24%

news.title: LeBron James Responds to President Donald Trump’s Criticism of His Behavior During National Anthem
news.text:
LeBron James seemingly is not taking President Donald Trump's latest personal jabs seriously as debate swirls over the athlete's behavior during a recent NBA game.
"It's a slow news day at the office, you know," James, 41, told reporters in the locker room following the Philadelphia 76ers' 114-106 win over the Cleveland Cavaliers on Thursday, October 22.
Trump, 80, seized on a new controversy involving James when the NBA star was shown on camera practicing taking golf swings and warming up while the National Anthem was played before the 76ers' season opener against the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday, October 20. (The 76ers beat the reigning NBA Champions, the Knicks, 106-100 in James' debut for the franchise.)
"While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country," Trump complained via Truth Social hours later. "I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE. LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for."
The president continued to attack James during his rally in Sioux City on Wednesday, October 22, asking why the 76ers power forward "[left] the court while the National Anthem was playing."
"What's that about?" Trump asked a booing crowd. "The NFL did that for a while and they stopped because people stopped watching the games."
76ers coach Nick Nurse brushed off Trump's criticism of James before Thursday's game, insisting the chatter "goes right in with other outside noise we've already had."
"All I really care about is getting them to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor, and the focus that they've had and the intent and all the stuff they've had has been excellent," Nurse, 59, told the media.
Trump and James' feud dates back nearly a decade to the NBA legend branding the president "a bum" for rescinding a White House invitation for Stephen Curry to visit with the Golden State Warriors in 2017. James has endorsed all three of Trump's presidential election challengers — Hillary Clinton in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024.
"When I think about my kids and my family and how they will grow up, the choice is clear to me. VOTE KAMALA HARRIS," James tweeted in October 2024.
The president fired back by speculating that the newly-signed 76ers player might be "racist" in July when asked whether James or Michael Jordan is the true NBA GOAT.
“Michael Jordan’s a guy that’s a friend of mine,” Trump insisted. “I play golf with him. He’s a really good guy.”
He added, "And I think LeBron, maybe he’s a racist. But maybe he doesn’t like Trump. I don’t know. I only like people that like me, so I would say Michael Jordan all the way."
Trump offered no context for why he accused James of racism at the time.
news.author: Justin Harp

news.title: Trump Political Org Pours Millions Into Florida District Race After House GOP PAC Slashed Funding
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s political operation planned to spend money in a competitive House race Thursday after Republicans slashed funding in the district. 

The No Going Back PAC, a super PAC backed by MAGA Inc., is pouring more than $25 million into House races, including $6.3 million in Florida’s 25th district where they hope to defeat Democratic Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz, Punchbowl News first reported. The Congressional Leadership Fund, the top House super PAC, slashed $6 million in planned advertising to oppose Moskowitz and redirected $9 million to defend House seats held by Republicans. (RELATED: Senate Republicans’ Top PAC Dropping $1 Million Into Deep-Red Mississippi)

The super PAC planned to spend $1 million in Washington’s third district, $85,000 in Florida’s 22nd district, $1 million in Florida’s 14th district and $1.2 million in Montana’s first district. 

NEW: buys are starting to trickle in from No Going Back PAC >> $6.3M in #FL25 to target Jared Moskowitz (D) >> $1M in #WA03 to target MGP (D) >> $85K so far in open #FL22 for Casey Askar (R) >> $1M in #FL14 to target Kathy Castor (D) >>$1.2M in open #MT01 for Aaron Flint (R)— Ally Mutnick (@allymutnick) October 22, 2026

Moskowitz is running against former Republican Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer, who served as mayor for eight years. He campaigned on delivering “common-sense, America First policies” and standing up against “a radical far-left agenda,” according to his campaign website. 

Cook Political Report moved the race from the “Toss Up” column to “Lean Democratic.” Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the race’s rating in Moskowitz’s favor. 

Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis unveiled a newly drawn congressional map on May 4 that would help Republicans gain four seats. The map intended to benefit Republicans in the 25th district as it no longer covers its former inland Broward County areas.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Florida’s 25th district in a 52.1% to 46.8% margin in the 2024 election. Democratic Florida Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz won the district in 2024 by a 54.5% to 45.5% margin.

Moskowitz defeated his further-left opponent Oliver Larkin in the Aug. 18 primary, despite Larkin receiving endorsements from members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Candidates backed by the DSA won several of their races against their incumbent challengers throughout the 2026 primary cycle, including 29-year-old Melat Kiros in Colorado’s first district.

Cook Political Report shifted 19 House races in Democrats’ favor, including four Republican-held seats in Arizona, Colorado, Wisconsin and Virginia.
news.summary: Republicans slashed $6 million in the district

news.title: 'The Simpsons' resurrects Apu after nearly a decade of silence
news.text: Across 38 seasons of "The Simpsons," the Halloween-themed "Treehouse of Horror" episodes have always been a treat of spooky stand-alone storylines. On Sunday, the show surprised viewers with a major resurrection: Apu, the beloved Kwik-E-Mart operator who had not been heard for the better part of a decade, spoke once again in Springfield.He and his wife, Manjula, were back with a meaty plotline — and the voices of actual Indian American actors: Sunil Malhotra, a veteran voice-over artist, and Janina Gavankar ("The Morning Show")."Bringing Apu back feels like a reclamation. It truly IS his homecoming," Malhotra and Gavankar said Sunday in a joint Instagram post.RECENT ENTERTAINMENT NEWS | Glee reboot officially ordered at Disney+ and HuluApu's unheralded return is a remarkable twist to a yearslong discourse about how the character has represented a painful stereotype for some South Asian Americans. After a 2017 documentary by comedian Hari Kondabolu, "The Problem With Apu," the character was largely exiled from the screen.In "The Problem With Apu," Kondabolu, a self-described fan of the Fox show, tried to process his misgivings. He interviewed a slew of celebrities of South Asian origin, including Kal Penn, Utkarsh Ambudkar and Hasan Minhaj, about growing up with the character. They shared memories of being bullied and called "Apu" as an insult. Adding to their view of Apu as just a caricature was that Hank Azaria, a white actor, voiced him.With the full name of Apu Nahasapeemapetilon Jr., he felt like the "forever foreigner, someone who represents Indians in the United States through this sole typology of being a convenience store owner, being a recent immigrant, having this heavy accent, being really limited in this sort of like American identity," says Bhoomi Thakore, an assistant professor of sociology at the University of Connecticut. Thakore notes that Kondabolu's film raised the notion that Apu was the only portrayal of an Indian character most people knew when he debuted in 1990.Azaria stepped away from the role after the documentary, continuing to voice other "Simpsons" characters, as Apu fell silent, seen only in the background. Kondabolu, however, had never called for Apu to be canceled. On Monday, he praised "The Simpsons" for devising "a clever solution to all this" and hiring Malhotra and Gavankar.MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS | 'Widow’s Bay' makes Emmy history while 'The Pitt' underwhelms"I'm also still proud of the public conversation about race and representation my documentary started," he told The Associated Press in an emailed statement. "Finally, I'm hoping this stops all the hatemail in many languages that has been sent my way over the past decade."In a 2018 episode, "The Simpsons" responded to Kondabolu's documentary by having Lisa Simpson bemoan how "something that started decades ago and was applauded and inoffensive is now politically incorrect. ... What can you do?" The camera then panned to a framed photo of Apu. The gag was branded by some as weak for not directly addressing the controversy.In a 2020 New York Times interview, Azaria, who by then hadn't voiced Apu in a few years, announced he would bow out because "it just didn't feel right." Later that year, in response to racial reckoning demonstrations, "The Simpsons" announced it would no longer cast white voice actors as characters of color. The show then recast two Black characters, Carl Carlson and Dr. Julius Hibbert, with Black actors.Kondabolu had not spoken with "The Simpsons" producers about Apu's comeback, he confirmed to the AP, "but they didn't owe me that." And it does sound like Apu is here to stay."We love this character and wanted to bring him back in a smart, Simpsons-y way that allowed him to evolve," executive producer Matt Selman said in a statement. "We're excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future."A few weeks after "The Simpsons" responded to the documentary, author and producer Amar Shah wrote a series of social media posts and then a Washington Post op-ed on why he felt mostly sentimental toward Apu. When he watched Apu, he thought of his own Indian father hard at work as a convenience store owner and how that shaped his Florida childhood."Apu even now is a character that I wouldn't mind my kids seeing represented because they'll see aspects of themselves and of their own grandparents," says Shah, reflecting on his 2018 piece. "I can totally empathize with someone of South Asian origin having a different POV (point of view) than me but this is my childhood. This is my story."After watching this latest episode, Shah didn't sense any significant difference with Malhotra's performance."Obviously, there's a different voice, tenor, texture and all that. But, the character is always going to be there, his genuine humanity," Shah says. "I think if they had incorporated this change earlier, it would have been a lot better."Apu is being revived amid a climate of rising anti-South Asian and Indian hate. Stop AAPI Hate and other research groups have found online use of racist slurs and threats against South Asians and Indians have jumped in the past few years.Texas Railroad Commission candidate Bo French, a Republican, recently posted a photo of South Asian University of Texas students cheering at a football game and called them "a problem." Just last week, a man was charged with planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple outside Chicago. Against that backdrop, Shah welcomes the show's careful approach reincarnating the character."It's great to see that the show has evolved in time and now, especially with the discrimination and, really, the targeting of South Asians and Indian Americans as of late — questioning our patriotism, our American identity and even whether we're college football fans," he says.The return also coincides with much more representation of prominent South Asian Americans, such as actor and showrunner Mindy Kaling, and people who have broken barriers in office, like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former Vice President Kamala Harris.When Apu first appeared, says University of Virginia associate professor of media studies Shilpa Davé, he was one of the only consistent representations of South Asians on TV.Now, she says, "South Asians have become a part of the landscape from 'Bridgerton' to … 'Never Have I Ever' and there's a plethora of different kinds of representation."
news.summary: On Sunday, the show surprised viewers with a major resurrection: Apu, the beloved Kwik-E-Mart operator who had not been heard for the better part of a decade, spoke once again in Springfield.
news.author: AP via Scripps News Group
